title: Playing fair: games and rules

summary.text: Ten tamarind seeds lie on the floor. Are they a game yet? In this lesson you find out that a game begins only when the players agree on a rule and keep it. You meet indoor and outdoor games from all over India, and you learn how to take turns, play safely, and win and lose kindly. You also find out that dogs, rats and bees play too, and that scientists still argue about what 'fair' and 'play' really mean.
summary.art: Ten brown tamarind seeds in a heap on a red oxide floor, with a child on one side and a grown-up on the other, both looking at the seeds.

intro.hook: Put ten tamarind seeds, or ten beans, in a heap on the floor. Look at them. Is this a game? If not, what is missing?
intro.text: Right now the seeds are only seeds. Now say these words to the person beside you: 'We take turns. On your turn you take one seed or two seeds. Whoever takes the last seed wins.' Play it once. You did not add anything to the floor, but now there is a game. Today you will find out what you added. You will also ask what happens to a game when one player stops keeping the rule.
intro.art: Ten brown tamarind seeds in a small heap on a red oxide floor, with a child's open hand on one side and a grown-up's open hand on the other, both waiting.

outcomes: By the end I can say what makes a game a game: rules that all the players agree to keep.
By the end I can name indoor games and outdoor games, including games from different parts of India, and say one rule of each.
By the end I can take turns, and say why a turn rule gives every player a go.
By the end I can say two different things that 'fair' can mean, and give an example of each.
By the end I can name two safety rules for play, and say which part of the body each rule protects.
By the end I can win and lose kindly, and say why a game needs the player who loses as much as the player who wins.
By the end I can tell how a dog or a rat keeps rules in play, and name one question about play that nobody can answer yet.

explanations.concept: A game is play with rules that every player agrees to keep
explanations.definition: A game is a kind of play that has rules. A rule is a sentence that says what a player may do, must do or must not do. All the players know the rules and agree to keep them.
explanations.description: Think of kannamoochi, which is the Tamil name for hide and seek. One child is the seeker. She must shut her eyes and count to twenty. The others must hide before she finishes. Those are rules. Nobody can see a rule or pick it up. A rule lives in what the players say and do. If the seeker peeps through her fingers, the hiding is spoiled for everyone. Most games also have a goal, which is the thing the players are trying to do. The seeker's goal is to find everyone. The rules say how she is allowed to reach that goal.
examples: In carrom, the rule says you flick the striker with a finger. You may not push a coin into the pocket with your hand.
In the seed game with ten seeds, the rule says you take one seed or two on your turn. Taking three is against the rule.
In kho-kho, the chaser may run in only one direction along the line of sitting players.
Building a tower of blocks alone is play. It becomes a game when you add a rule, such as 'we take turns and the one who makes it fall loses'.

perspectives.who: Johan Huizinga, a Dutch historian, in his book 'Homo Ludens' of 1938
perspectives.explanation: He wrote that a game makes a small world of its own. It has its own place, such as a chalk square or a board. It has its own time, with a start and an end. Inside that world the rules are the only law, and the players follow them by choice.

perspectives.who: Ludwig Wittgenstein, a philosopher, in 'Philosophical Investigations', sections 66 and 67, published in 1953
perspectives.explanation: He asked his readers to look at board games, card games, ball games and a child throwing a ball at a wall. He found no single thing that all of them share. Some have winners and some do not. Some need skill and some need luck. He said games are like the members of a family, who look alike in different ways. So the word 'game' may have no exact definition at all.

explanations.art: Children playing hide and seek in a courtyard: one girl counting with her hands over her eyes, with a faint speech bubble showing the rule 'count to 20' above her.
explanations.context: This card says what a game is and what a rule is, before the lesson uses those two words.

explanations.concept: The same seeds become a different game when the rule changes
explanations.definition: The things you play with do not decide the game. The rules decide the game.
explanations.description: Take a handful of tamarind seeds. With one set of rules they are pallanguzhi, a game from Tamil Nadu. In pallanguzhi the seeds sit in a board with 14 small pits, and you drop them into the pits one by one. With another rule the same seeds become 'odd or even'. You hide some seeds in your fist, and your friend guesses if the number is odd or even. With a third rule you toss one seed up and pick another from the floor before you catch it. The seeds did not change. The rule changed, so the game changed. This also works the other way. You can keep the rules and change the things. Pallanguzhi can be played with shells, pebbles or beans.
examples: One ball can be used for football, where only the feet may touch it, and for catch, where only the hands do.
One pack of playing cards is used for hundreds of different games.
Some chess players can play with their eyes covered. They keep the whole board in their heads and say each move aloud. They have no pieces to touch, and it is still chess.

perspectives.who: Bernard Suits, a philosopher, in his book 'The Grasshopper' of 1978
perspectives.explanation: He noticed that game rules make things harder on purpose. The easy way to get a football into the goal is to carry it there in your hands. The rule forbids that, and the fun comes from the rule. He said that playing a game means choosing to get past obstacles that you did not need to have.

perspectives.who: Mathematicians who study games, beginning with John von Neumann in 1928
perspectives.explanation: For them a game is its rules and nothing more: who the players are, which moves each may make, and what each gets at the end. The board and the pieces are only a way to remember where the game has reached.

explanations.art: One heap of tamarind seeds in the middle, with three arrows leading to three small scenes: seeds in a pallanguzhi board, seeds hidden in a closed fist, and one seed in the air above a child's hand.
explanations.context: This card shows that rules, and not the playing pieces, make one game different from another.

explanations.concept: Players make the rules, and players can change them if everyone agrees
explanations.definition: Game rules are made by people. They can be changed when all the players agree to the change before they play.
explanations.description: In one lane, children playing hide and seek count to 20. In the next lane they count to 50. In one home, nobody may hide inside the house. In another home that is allowed. Neither is wrong. Each group agreed on its own rule. You can change a rule too. Say the new rule aloud before the game starts, and ask if everyone agrees. Changing a rule in the middle, without asking, is different. It usually helps the one who changed it, and the others feel cheated. When teams from far-away places play a match, they need the same rules. So a group of people writes one rule book for everyone. Kabaddi, kho-kho and cricket each have a written rule book.
examples: Before a game of ludo, a family agrees: 'You need a six to bring a token out.' Another family agrees that any number will do.
Two friends agree that in their race the younger one starts three steps ahead.
In a kabaddi match played to the written rules, each side has seven players on the court.

perspectives.who: Jean Piaget, a Swiss scientist, in 'The Moral Judgment of the Child', 1932
perspectives.explanation: He sat on the ground with boys in Geneva and Neuchâtel, played marbles with them and asked where the rules came from. The younger boys said the rules had always been there and could never be changed, though they often broke them. Boys of about ten said the rules were an agreement between players, and that a new rule was fine if everyone accepted it.

perspectives.who: Iona Opie and Peter Opie, in 'Children's Games in Street and Playground', 1969
perspectives.explanation: They collected games from thousands of children across Britain. They found that children teach games to other children, with no grown-up and no rule book. The same game had slightly different rules from one town to the next, and the children of each town were sure that theirs were the right ones.

perspectives.who: Janet Lever in 1976 and Carol Gilligan in 1982, researchers in the United States
perspectives.explanation: Piaget had judged the girls he watched to be less interested in rules than the boys. Lever watched children of about ten at play. She saw that when a quarrel began, the girls often stopped the game, while the boys argued about the rule and went on. Gilligan said the girls were not weaker at rules. They were putting the friendship ahead of the game. So the same playground can be read in two ways.

explanations.art: Two groups of children on two sides of a lane, each playing hide and seek, one seeker's bubble showing '20' and the other's showing '50'.
explanations.context: This card answers the question 'who decides the rules?' and shows the right way to change one.

explanations.concept: Cheating is breaking a rule in secret while the others keep it
explanations.definition: To cheat is to break a rule on purpose, and hide it, so that you get ahead of players who are keeping the rule.
explanations.description: A girl playing ludo rolls a three. She moves her token four squares while nobody is looking. She has cheated. Look at what the cheat needs. She needs the other players to go on keeping the rule. If everyone moved as many squares as they liked, moving four would win her nothing. So a cheat uses the other players' honesty. When they find out, they stop trusting her, and often they stop playing with her. A mistake is different from cheating. If you forget a rule, you can say 'sorry, I forgot' and put the token back. Breaking a rule openly is different again. A child who kicks over the board has not cheated. That child has ended the game.
examples: Peeping through your fingers while you count in hide and seek is cheating.
Saying 'I was not out!' when you know the ball touched you is cheating.
Miscounting your squares by accident, and going back when someone points it out, is a mistake.

perspectives.who: Johan Huizinga, in 'Homo Ludens', 1938
perspectives.explanation: He wrote that players are often angrier with the spoilsport than with the cheat. The cheat still pretends to play, so the little world of the game stays standing. The spoilsport walks out or kicks the board, and the world of the game is gone.

perspectives.who: The Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, the story of the game of dice
perspectives.explanation: King Yudhishthira plays dice against Shakuni, who is known to play with tricks. Yudhishthira loses his kingdom, his brothers and himself, and then stakes his wife Draupadi and loses again. Draupadi stands in the hall and asks a question about the rules: can a man who has already lost himself stake anyone else? The elders cannot answer her. The epic shows a game that was unfair from the start, and a woman who was the one to question its rules.

perspectives.who: Marc Bekoff, an American scientist who studies dogs, coyotes and wolves at play
perspectives.explanation: He saw that a young coyote who invites another to play and then bites hard is avoided afterwards. The others stop accepting that coyote's invitations. So cheating at play costs other animals their playmates too.

explanations.art: A ludo board seen from above with one child's hand sliding a token one square too far, while the other players look away at the dice.
explanations.context: This card says what cheating is, how it differs from a mistake, and why it harms the game for everyone.

explanations.concept: Indoor games fit in a room, and outdoor games need open space
explanations.definition: An indoor game can be played inside a room. An outdoor game needs open space, such as a playground, a lane, a courtyard or a terrace.
explanations.description: Carrom, chess, ludo, pallanguzhi and five stones are indoor games. You sit, and you use your fingers, your eyes and your memory. They need little room, and rain does not stop them. Kabaddi, kho-kho, cricket, football and tag are outdoor games. You run, jump, throw and dodge. Your heart beats faster and you breathe harder, because your muscles are asking for more air and food. Both kinds make you think. A carrom player plans her shot. A kho-kho runner plans which way to turn. The two groups are not walled off from each other. Hopscotch can be chalked in a corridor, and five stones can be played on a doorstep.
examples: Antakshari is an indoor singing game. Each player sings a song that starts with the last sound of the song before.
Lagori, also called seven stones, is an outdoor game. One team knocks down a pile of seven flat stones with a ball and tries to build it again before being hit.
On a rainy day in Kochi, a game of statues in the front room gives the whole body a run, though it is indoors.

perspectives.who: School syllabuses in India, such as the ICSE Class 1 syllabus
perspectives.explanation: They sort games by place: indoor or outdoor. This is a handy way to choose a game for the room, the weather and the number of players you have.

perspectives.who: Sports scientists, who study how bodies move
perspectives.explanation: They sort games by what the body does: active games that make the heart beat fast, and sitting games. By this sorting, kabaddi played on a mat inside a hall is still an active game, and a quiet word game played under a tree is still a sitting game. The place matters less than the movement.

explanations.art: A house cut open like a doll's house: inside, two children at a carrom board, and outside in the lane, four children playing seven stones with a small pile of flat stones and a ball.
explanations.context: This card sorts games into indoor and outdoor, and shows that the sorting depends on what you choose to look at.

explanations.concept: One game has many names across India
explanations.definition: Children in every part of India play games. Many of the same games are played in different places under different names, with small changes in the rules.
explanations.description: Hop on one foot through chalk squares and you are playing a game with many names. It is nondi or paandi in Tamil Nadu, kunte bille in Karnataka, tokkudu billa in Telugu, ekka dokka in Bengal and kith-kith or stapu in the north. The pile of seven stones is lagori in Karnataka, pittu in the north and satodiyu in Gujarat. Other games belong to one region. Aadu puli aattam, the game of goats and tigers, is a board game from South India with 3 tigers and 15 goats. Kumir danga is a tag game from Bengal, where one child is the crocodile in the 'water'. Yubi lakpi from Manipur is played with a coconut that the players try to carry to the goal.
examples: Five stones is played sitting on the floor. You toss one stone up, pick another from the floor and catch the first stone before it lands.
Gilli danda is played with a short stick and a long stick. In Kerala a game of the same kind is called kuttiyum kolum.
Kabaddi needs no ball, no bat and no board. It needs only a line on the ground and two teams.
Pallanguzhi belongs to a family of pit-and-seed games played across Africa and Asia. In Ghana a game of this family is called oware.

perspectives.who: Children on each street, as Iona and Peter Opie found in Britain in 1969
perspectives.explanation: Each group of children is sure that the name and the rules they use are the real ones. Children in the next town are just as sure about theirs.

perspectives.who: Historians of games
perspectives.explanation: They ask if a game was invented once and carried from place to place, or invented many times by different children. For hopscotch, tag and hide and seek, nobody knows. No record tells us who played them first.

explanations.art: A simple map of India with six small pictures placed on it: hopscotch squares in the south, a pile of seven stones in the west, a crocodile tag game in the east, a coconut in the north-east, kabaddi players in the north and a goats-and-tigers board at the tip.
explanations.context: This card names games children play in different parts of India, and shows how one game travels under many names.

explanations.concept: Some very old games from India are now played around the world
explanations.definition: Chess, ludo, and snakes and ladders all grew from games first played in India. Dice have been found in Indian cities that are more than 4,000 years old.
explanations.description: People who dug up the old cities of Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Lothal found small cubes with dots on each face. They are dice, made about 4,500 years ago. So people here were playing games then. Chess grew from an Indian game called chaturanga, played by about the 6th century CE. Its pieces were the four parts of an army: foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots. Ludo grew from pachisi, played on a cloth board shaped like a plus sign, with cowrie shells thrown as dice. Snakes and ladders grew from gyan chaupar. On those old boards each ladder stood for a good deed and each snake for a harmful one. Travellers and traders carried all three games to other countries.
examples: From India, chaturanga went to Persia, then to the Arab world, and then to Europe, changing a little at each step.
A board game called Ludo, based on pachisi, was registered in England in 1896.
The oldest gyan chaupar boards that still exist were painted in the 1700s. The game may be much older, but no older board has been found.

perspectives.who: The Brahmajala Sutta, the first discourse of the Digha Nikaya, a Buddhist text more than 2,000 years old
perspectives.explanation: It gives one of the oldest lists of games anywhere. It names board games with eight or ten rows of squares, the same games played in the mind with no board, hopping games, dice, hitting a short stick with a long one, and guessing letters drawn in the air. The text says the Buddha did not spend his time on these. For us it is a record that people in India played them.

perspectives.who: Most historians of chess, following H. J. R. Murray's 'A History of Chess', 1913
perspectives.explanation: They trace chess to chaturanga in north India. They point to the Sanskrit names of the pieces and to the path the game took through Persia.

perspectives.who: A smaller group of historians
perspectives.explanation: They argue that chess may have begun in China or in Central Asia, or grew up along the trade routes between them and India. The earliest writings are few, so the question is not fully closed.

explanations.art: Three pairs of pictures joined by arrows: a four-part army board beside a modern chess board, a plus-shaped cloth with cowrie shells beside a ludo board, and a painted board of snakes and ladders with tiny writing in each square beside a modern one.
explanations.context: This card tells how old games are, and which world-famous board games began in India.

explanations.concept: Some games are won by luck, some by skill, and most by both
explanations.definition: Luck is what happens by chance, such as the number a dice shows. Skill is what you get better at with practice. A game can depend on luck, on skill, or on a mix of the two.
explanations.description: In snakes and ladders you make no choices. The dice decides every move. A child playing for the first time has the same chance as a player of fifty years. That is a game of luck. In chess there are no dice at all. Every move is a choice, and the player who plans better usually wins. That is a game of skill. Most games sit in between. In ludo the dice gives the number, but you choose which token to move. In carrom your aim matters most, but a coin can still bounce in an odd way. This tells you something about winning. If you win a game of luck, you were lucky. If you win a game of skill, you played well today.
examples: Tossing a coin to see who starts is pure luck. Each side has an equal chance.
In five stones, the same child gets better week by week. That shows skill.
In a card game, the cards you are dealt are luck. How you play them is skill.

perspectives.who: The makers of gyan chaupar boards in India
perspectives.explanation: They made a game with no choices on purpose. Nobody can stay on top by being clever, and a fall down a snake can come to anyone. The board was a picture of how a life goes up and down.

perspectives.who: The Mahabharata, Vana Parva, the story of Nala
perspectives.explanation: King Rituparna looks at a tree and tells the number of its leaves and fruits without counting them all. He says this skill and the skill of dice are one knowledge, and he teaches it to Nala. So an old Indian story treats dice as something that can be understood with numbers, and not only as fate.

perspectives.who: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat, French mathematicians, in letters of 1654
perspectives.explanation: A friend asked them how to share the prize of a dice game that had to stop early. Working it out, they began the maths of chance, which is now called probability. So luck itself follows patterns that can be counted.

explanations.art: A line with a dice at the left end and a chess queen at the right end, and four games placed along it: snakes and ladders nearest the dice, then ludo, then carrom, then chess.
explanations.context: This card separates luck from skill, which changes what a win or a loss tells you.

explanations.concept: Taking turns gives every player a go
explanations.definition: Taking turns means one player acts while the others wait, and then the next player acts. The turn goes round until everyone has had a go.
explanations.description: Two children cannot both flick the carrom striker at once. So the rule says: you, then me, then you. A turn rule shares out the playing time. Without one, the fastest or the strongest child takes every go, and the rest only watch. You were taking turns long before you played your first game. When two people talk, one speaks and the other listens, and then they swap. People who study talking have timed this. The gap between one speaker and the next is usually about a fifth of a second. That is shorter than a blink. To be that quick, the listener must guess when the speaker is about to stop.
examples: On a swing, a turn can be counted: twenty swings each, and then the next child.
In a board game the turn goes round the circle, usually to the left or to the right, and it never skips a player.
In kabaddi the two teams take turns to send a raider across the line.

perspectives.who: Mary Catherine Bateson, an American scientist, in 1975
perspectives.explanation: She filmed mothers with babies about two months old. The baby cooed, the mother answered, and the baby waited and cooed again. She called it a 'proto-conversation', which means a first kind of talking. Babies take turns before they know a single word.

perspectives.who: Tanya Stivers and a team of language scientists, in 2009
perspectives.explanation: They timed the gaps between speakers in ten languages from different parts of the world. In all ten, people mostly avoided talking over each other, and most gaps were close to a fifth of a second.

perspectives.who: Daniel Takahashi, Asif Ghazanfar and their team, who study marmoset monkeys, in 2013
perspectives.explanation: Marmosets are small monkeys from Brazil. When two marmosets cannot see each other, they call back and forth. Each one waits about five seconds after the other finishes before calling. They do not call over each other. Turn-taking is found in other animals and is not a human invention.

explanations.art: Two children at a carrom board, with a curved arrow going from one child's hand to the other's and back again, marked '1, 2, 1, 2'.
explanations.context: This card says what taking turns is, and shows that babies and monkeys do it too.

explanations.concept: Waiting for a turn is easier when you trust that your turn will come
explanations.definition: Waiting is hard work for the body and the mind. Children can wait longer when the people around them keep their word.
explanations.description: Waiting for your turn can feel bad. Your hands want to grab and your legs want to go. In 2013 a scientist named Celeste Kidd tested what makes waiting easier. Each child of three to five years was promised better art materials by a grown-up. For half the children, the grown-up kept the promise. For the other half, the grown-up came back with nothing. Then every child was given one marshmallow, a soft sweet, and was told: wait, and you will get two. Children who had met the promise-keeper waited about 12 minutes. Children who had met the promise-breaker waited about 3 minutes. So waiting depends a lot on trust. A turn rule that everyone keeps makes waiting easier for all.
examples: When turns on the swing are counted aloud, the waiting child can hear her turn coming nearer.
A child who was skipped last time finds it harder to wait this time.
Singing, counting or watching the other player's move makes a wait feel shorter.

perspectives.who: Walter Mischel and his team at Stanford University, in studies from 1970 to 1972
perspectives.explanation: They ran the first marshmallow tests. Children who covered their eyes, sang or thought of something else waited longer than children who stared at the sweet. They saw waiting as a skill inside the child that can be practised.

perspectives.who: Celeste Kidd, Holly Palmeri and Richard Aslin, at the University of Rochester, in 2013
perspectives.explanation: They showed that the same child waits or does not wait depending on how reliable the grown-up has been. A child who grabs the sweet may be making a sensible choice in a world where promises are broken. They saw waiting as something between the child and the people around the child.

explanations.art: A child standing beside a swing, counting on her fingers while another child swings, with small numbers 18, 19, 20 floating above the swing.
explanations.context: This card looks at why waiting for a turn is hard, and what a real test found about making it easier.

explanations.concept: 'Fair' has more than one meaning, and people do not agree on one
explanations.definition: A game or a sharing is called fair when no player is treated worse than another without a good reason. People disagree about what counts as a good reason.
explanations.description: Three ideas of fair are common. The first is 'the same for everyone': each child gets two laddus. The second is 'more for the one who needs more': the child who missed lunch gets an extra laddu. The third is 'more for the one who did more': the child who helped to roll the laddus gets an extra one. Each idea sounds fair. They can give three different answers for the same plate of laddus. Games mostly use the first idea. Everyone follows the same rules and gets the same number of turns. But think of a race between a child of six and a child of ten. Starting from the same line is 'the same for everyone'. Giving the younger child a head start is 'more for the one who needs more'. Which race is the fair one?
examples: A coin toss to decide who goes first gives both players the same chance.
In a family game of cricket, the smallest child is allowed three misses before she is out.
Two children share one dosa. One cuts it, and the other chooses a piece first. The cutter then tries hard to make the pieces equal.

perspectives.who: Amartya Sen, an Indian economist, in 'The Idea of Justice', 2009
perspectives.explanation: He tells of three children and one flute. Anne says she should have it because she is the only one who can play it. Bob says he should have it because he has no toys at all. Carla says she should have it because she made it. Sen says each child has a strong reason, and no single rule shows that the other two are wrong.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek philosopher, in the 'Nicomachean Ethics', book 5, about 340 BCE
perspectives.explanation: He held that fair shares are in proportion. People who did the same should get the same, and people who did more should get more.

perspectives.who: John Rawls, an American philosopher, in 'A Theory of Justice', 1971
perspectives.explanation: He said a rule is fair if you would agree to it before you knew which player you were going to be. The dosa rule works this way. The child who cuts does not know which piece she will get, so she cuts evenly.

explanations.art: A plate of five laddus between three children, drawn three times with different sharings: equal piles, a bigger pile for a hungry-looking child, and a bigger pile for a child with flour on her hands.
explanations.context: This card shows that 'fair' can mean the same for all, more for need, or more for effort, and that the word has no single agreed meaning.

explanations.concept: Children all over the world mind getting less, but minding getting more depends on where they grow up
explanations.definition: In every place scientists have tested, young children refuse a share that is smaller than another child's. Refusing a share that is bigger than another child's appears later, and only in some places.
explanations.description: In 2015 a team led by Peter Blake and Katherine McAuliffe tested hundreds of pairs of children aged 4 to 15. The children lived in seven countries: India, Uganda, Senegal, Peru, Mexico, Canada and the United States. Two children sat at a machine with two trays of sweets. One child had a handle. She could accept the trays, or she could reject them, and then nobody got any sweets. Sometimes her tray had 1 sweet and the other child's had 4. In all seven countries, children learned to reject that. They chose nothing for both over less for themselves. Sometimes her tray had 4 and the other child's had 1. Only older children in three of the countries rejected that. So one part of fairness shows up everywhere. Another part seems to be learned from the people around us.
examples: A child of five who gets the smaller half of a chikki says 'That's not fair!' at once.
The same child may say nothing when she is the one who gets the bigger half.
An older child sometimes gives back the extra, saying 'We should have the same.'

perspectives.who: Ernst Fehr, Helen Bernhard and Bettina Rockenbach, in a study of Swiss children published in 2008
perspectives.explanation: They let children of 3 to 8 choose how to share sweets with another child. Most children of 3 and 4 chose what was best for themselves. By 7 and 8, many more chose equal shares. They concluded that the wish for equal shares grows strongly between those ages.

perspectives.who: Peter Blake, Katherine McAuliffe and their team, in the seven-country study of 2015
perspectives.explanation: They agree that fairness grows with age. They add that it does not grow the same way everywhere. Giving up your own extra share appeared in only three of their seven countries. They do not yet know which habits of each place make the difference.

perspectives.who: Christina Starmans, Mark Sheskin and Paul Bloom, in a paper of 2017
perspectives.explanation: They argue that children and grown-ups do not really want equal shares. They want fair shares. When one child has done more of the work, even young children often give that child more. So the three meanings of fair are already at work in childhood.

explanations.art: Two children facing each other across a small wooden machine with two trays, one tray holding one sweet and the other four, and one child's hand on a handle.
explanations.context: This card reports what tests found about children's feeling for fairness in seven countries, including India.

explanations.concept: Every win needs someone who lost, so winners and losers both keep the game going
explanations.definition: In a game with a winner, somebody else has not won. Winning kindly and losing kindly are the ways players treat each other so that both want to play again.
explanations.description: You cannot win hide and seek alone. To win, you need another player who tried and did not win this time. So the one who lost has given you something: a real game. Losing can sting. Your face may feel hot and your chest tight. Those feelings are real, and they pass. A kind loser says 'Well played' and may ask for another round. A kind winner is glad without teasing, and thanks the other player. A winner who boasts and a loser who throws the pieces do the same harm. They make the other player not want to come back. A scientist named Jaak Panksepp saw this in young rats who play-wrestle. When the stronger rat pinned the weaker one every time, the weaker rat stopped wanting to play.
examples: After a kabaddi match, the two teams line up and shake hands.
A girl who wins at carrom says, 'That last shot of yours was good. Shall we play again?'
A boy who loses at ludo takes three slow breaths, and then helps to set the tokens out for the next game.

perspectives.who: The Bhagavad Gita, chapter 2, verse 38
perspectives.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat alike, and then to act. Many readers take from this that a person should do the thing well and hold the result lightly.

perspectives.who: Jaak Panksepp, in 'Affective Neuroscience', 1998, and Sergio Pellis and Vivien Pellis, in 'The Playful Brain', 2009
perspectives.explanation: These scientists watched rats play-wrestle. Panksepp reported that the stronger rat has to let the weaker one win some of the time, about 3 rounds in 10, or the weaker one stops joining in. The Pellises showed that rats hold back and leave openings for the partner. In rats, as in children, play lasts only while both sides get something.

perspectives.who: Many coaches and players of competitive sport
perspectives.explanation: They say that trying your hardest to win is itself a way of respecting the other player. Going easy on purpose can feel like an insult. For them, kindness comes after the game, in the handshake, and not during it.

explanations.art: Two children on either side of a finished carrom board, one with more coins, reaching across to shake hands, both smiling.
explanations.context: This card is about winning and losing kindly, and why a game cannot do without the player who loses.

explanations.concept: In some games everyone wins or loses together
explanations.definition: In a competitive game the players try to beat each other. In a cooperative game all the players are on one side and try to beat a problem together.
explanations.description: Try to keep a balloon in the air with a friend, and count the taps. If the balloon touches the floor, you both lose. If you reach fifty taps, you both win. Nobody is beaten by anybody. This is a cooperative game. 'Cooperate' means to work together. Many games mix the two kinds. In kabaddi you compete against the other team, and you cooperate with your own team. A raider who is caught by seven hands is caught by seven players acting as one. Even two players who compete are cooperating in one way. They both keep the rules so that the game can happen.
examples: Two children turn a long skipping rope so that a third can jump. The three of them count the jumps together.
A family builds one tall tower of steel tumblers, each adding one in turn, to see how high it can go.
In lagori, the team that rebuilds the pile of seven stones wins or loses as a team.

perspectives.who: Terry Orlick, a Canadian sports scientist, in 'The Cooperative Sports and Games Book', 1978, and a study of 1981
perspectives.explanation: He gave one group of five-year-olds cooperative games for several weeks and another group ordinary games. Afterwards the children from the cooperative group were more willing to share sweets with other children.

perspectives.who: John Tauer and Judith Harackiewicz, American researchers, in 2004
perspectives.explanation: They tested children shooting basketballs alone against another child, as partners, and as teams against other teams. The children enjoyed it most, and often scored best, when they cooperated inside a team that was competing with another team. So competing and cooperating can work together.

explanations.art: Two children with arms stretched up, tapping a red balloon between them, with the count '27' written in the air.
explanations.context: This card names the two kinds of game, competitive and cooperative, and shows that most games hold some of each.

explanations.concept: Safety rules protect the players' bodies
explanations.definition: A safety rule is a rule that keeps players from getting hurt. Playing safely means keeping those rules and looking out for the other players.
explanations.description: Game rules say how to win. Safety rules say how to keep every body whole. Here are four that work for almost any game. First, look at the place. Wet floors, stairs, roads and sharp corners are not for running games. This protects your head, knees and teeth. Second, agree on a stop word. When anyone says 'Stop', every player stops at once. This protects whoever is hurt or scared. Third, in a chasing game you touch and never push. This protects backs and wrists. Fourth, drink water and rest in the shade on a hot day, because a hot, dry body tires fast and gets a headache. If someone is hurt, the game stops and a child fetches a grown-up. A game that hurts someone has stopped being play for that player.
examples: Before kho-kho on a terrace, the players check that the floor is dry and agree that nobody runs near the wall at the edge.
In cricket in the lane, the rule 'no hard hits towards the road' protects the players and the people passing by.
Small pieces such as carrom coins and marbles are kept away from babies, who may put them in their mouths.

perspectives.who: Torbjørn Soligard and a team of sports doctors in Norway, in a study published in 2008
perspectives.explanation: They followed about 1,900 girls aged 13 to 17 who played football. Half the clubs did a 20-minute warm-up of running, balancing and jumping exercises before playing. Those clubs had about one third fewer injuries. Getting the body ready is a safety rule that was measured.

perspectives.who: Marc Bekoff, who studies dogs, wolves and coyotes at play
perspectives.explanation: He points out that other animals keep safety rules too. Playing dogs hold back their bites. If one bites too hard, the other yelps, play stops for a moment, and the biter often bows as if to say sorry before play goes on.

explanations.art: A terrace with children about to play, and four small picture-signs along the wall: an eye for 'look first', an open palm for 'stop', a gentle tapping hand for 'touch, don't push', and a water bottle.
explanations.context: This card gives the safety rules that go with any game, and says which part of the body each one protects.

explanations.concept: Is a little risk in play good for children? Scientists disagree
explanations.definition: Risky play is exciting play in which a child could get hurt a little, such as climbing high, going fast or play-wrestling. Scientists disagree about how much of it children should have.
explanations.description: Climbing a guava tree is fun partly because you might slip. Some scientists say this kind of play teaches things that safe play cannot. A child who has climbed and wobbled learns how high is too high for her. Other scientists and doctors count the broken arms. Falls are a common reason for children's visits to hospital. They ask for softer ground, lower frames and a grown-up nearby. Both sides want children to be well. They disagree about where the line should be. One way to think about it is to tell a risk from a hazard. A risk is a danger that the child can see and choose, such as the height of a branch. A hazard is a danger the child cannot see, such as a rotten branch. Grown-ups can remove hazards and still leave some risks.
examples: Jumping from the second step is a risk a child can see and judge.
A loose slab on a wall is a hazard, because the child cannot tell that it will move.
Play-wrestling on a mattress, with a stop word, keeps the thrill and removes the hard floor.

perspectives.who: Ellen Beate Hansen Sandseter, a Norwegian researcher, in studies from 2007 to 2011
perspectives.explanation: She watched children in play schools and found that they seek out heights, speed and rough play again and again. With Leif Kennair she argued that this is how children lose their fear step by step and learn to judge danger. Children who are kept from all risk may stay more fearful.

perspectives.who: Mariana Brussoni and her team in Canada, in a review of 2015
perspectives.explanation: They read 21 studies on risky outdoor play. Taken together, the studies found more benefits than harms, such as more activity and better social skills. They also said that many of the studies were small and that better ones are needed.

perspectives.who: Doctors and groups who work to prevent children's injuries
perspectives.explanation: They point to hospital records, where falls from heights cause many broken bones and some serious head injuries. They hold that a lower climbing frame and a soft surface cost a child very little fun and can prevent a lasting injury.

explanations.art: A girl halfway up a guava tree, one foot testing a branch, with a grown-up below who is watching and not holding her.
explanations.context: This card gives both sides of a real disagreement about how safe play should be.

explanations.concept: Other animals play, and their play has rules too
explanations.definition: Many animals play, including dogs, rats, monkeys, crows and elephants. Their play has signals and rules that keep it friendly.
explanations.description: Watch two dogs before they play. One drops her front legs flat and keeps her back end up in the air. This is called a play bow. It is a signal that means 'What I do next is play. I am not attacking.' After the bow, the dogs chase, wrestle and nip softly. If one bites too hard, the game stops. Often the biter bows again, and play goes on. A big dog who plays with a small dog holds back her strength. She may even roll onto her back so that the small dog can be on top for a while. Then they swap. So dogs ask before they play, keep their bites gentle, say sorry and take turns. Those are rules, and nobody wrote them down.
examples: Two street dogs in a lane: one bows, the other bows back, and both dash off in a chase.
Young rhesus monkeys on a temple wall wrestle with their mouths open and relaxed, which is their play face.
Rats who are tickled make happy chirps that are too high for human ears to hear. A special microphone picks them up.

perspectives.who: Marc Bekoff, in a study of the play bow published in 1995, and with Jessica Pierce in 'Wild Justice', 2009
perspectives.explanation: He filmed dogs, wolves and coyotes at play and studied the films bit by bit. Bows came most often just before or just after a move that could be mistaken for a real attack, such as a bite with a head shake. He says the animals follow rules of fair play: ask first, be honest, hold back, and admit when you go too far.

perspectives.who: Annika Reinhold, Michael Brecht and their team in Berlin, in 2019
perspectives.explanation: They taught rats to play hide and seek with a person in a big room. The rats learned both jobs in a week or two. When hiding they stayed silent. When they found the person, or were found, they jumped and chirped. Their only reward was a tickle and more play. The rats kept the rules of each job.

perspectives.who: Scientists who are careful about reading minds from behaviour
perspectives.explanation: They agree about what the animals do. They say we cannot be sure that a dog thinks of the bow as a rule in the way a child thinks of a rule. The dog cannot tell us in words, so they prefer to say 'signal' and 'pattern' and leave the question open.

explanations.art: A brown street dog in a play bow, front legs flat and tail high, facing a smaller puppy who is copying the bow.
explanations.context: This card shows that play with rules is found in dogs and rats, and is not only a human thing.

explanations.concept: Do other animals feel 'that's not fair'? The tests are still argued over
explanations.definition: Some animals protest when a partner gets a better reward for the same work. Scientists disagree about what the protest means.
explanations.description: Other animals feel the difference when they are treated worse than a partner. In 2003, Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal tested this with capuchin monkeys, who are small monkeys from South America. Two female monkeys sat side by side. Each gave the scientist a small stone and was paid with a slice of cucumber. Both were content. Then one monkey was paid with a grape, which capuchins like far more. Her partner, still paid in cucumber, began to refuse. Sometimes she threw the cucumber back out of the cage. Some scientists read this differently. They say the monkey may simply be upset that a grape is in sight and she cannot have it. On that reading she is not comparing herself with her partner.
examples: A dog who watches another dog get a treat for 'shake hands', and gets nothing for the same trick, soon stops offering a paw.
A capuchin monkey who was happy with cucumber a minute ago refuses it once her neighbour is getting grapes.

perspectives.who: Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal, in 'Monkeys reject unequal pay', 2003
perspectives.explanation: They say the monkeys compare their own pay with a partner's and protest at getting less for the same work. They see this as an early form of the sense of fairness, shared by animals who live and work in groups.

perspectives.who: Juliane Bräuer, Josep Call and Michael Tomasello, in tests with chimpanzees and other apes from 2006
perspectives.explanation: They ran similar tests and did not find the same protest. They suggest the animals react to seeing a better food that they hoped for and did not get, whoever else is there. A true test, they say, must separate 'I got less than her' from 'I got less than I hoped'.

perspectives.who: Friederike Range and her team in Vienna, in a study of dogs in 2009
perspectives.explanation: They asked pairs of dogs to give a paw. A dog who got nothing while the partner was rewarded stopped giving the paw sooner than a dog who got nothing while alone. That points to the partner mattering. The dogs did not seem to mind a partner getting tastier food than theirs, so the picture is mixed.

explanations.art: Two capuchin monkeys in side-by-side clear boxes: one holding a grape, the other holding a slice of cucumber and looking across at the grape.
explanations.context: This card gives a famous test of fairness in monkeys and the honest argument about what it shows.

explanations.concept: What is play? Science has no final definition
explanations.definition: Play is a word everyone uses and nobody has defined exactly. Scientists use working tests to decide if an animal is playing, and they argue about where play stops.
explanations.description: You know play when you see it. Saying exactly what it is turns out to be hard. A scientist named Gordon Burghardt wrote five tests in 2005. The action is not needed for staying alive right now. The animal does it for its own sake. It looks like a serious action but is changed, for example a bite that does not hurt. It is done again and again. And it happens when the animal is fed, safe and relaxed. These tests are a working definition. They let scientists agree on what to count. With them, play has been reported in turtles, fish and octopuses. In 2022, bumblebees were added. Each bee rolled small wooden balls, though she got no food for doing it. Does a bee feel fun? Nobody can yet measure that. What do you think, and what would you test?
examples: A kitten pounces on a dry leaf. She is not hungry, and she does it again and again.
A crow slides down a sloping tin roof, flies back to the top and slides again.
At the Seattle Aquarium in the 1990s, two octopuses squirted water at a floating bottle so that it circled the tank and came back to them, many times over.

perspectives.who: Gordon Burghardt, in 'The Genesis of Animal Play', 2005
perspectives.explanation: He says play can be found with his five tests in many kinds of animals, including some with very different bodies from ours. He holds that play has appeared many times in the history of life.

perspectives.who: Samadi Galpayage Dona, Lars Chittka and their team in London, in 'Do bumble bees play?', 2022
perspectives.explanation: They watched 45 bumblebees who could walk past wooden balls to reach food. The bees went out of their way to roll the balls, some of them more than a hundred times. Younger bees rolled more than older ones, as young mammals play more than old ones. The team says this meets the tests for play.

perspectives.who: Scientists who want stronger proof
perspectives.explanation: They accept that the bees rolled the balls. They ask whether rolling could be practice for handling flowers, or a habit with no feeling in it. They note that a list of five tests describes what play looks like from outside and cannot show what it is like from inside.

perspectives.who: Jennifer Mather and Roland Anderson, who studied octopuses in 1999
perspectives.explanation: They reported the octopuses and the floating bottle. An octopus is a relative of snails and clams, and her ancestors parted from ours more than 50 crore years ago. If she plays, then play is either very old or has been invented more than once.

explanations.art: A row of five players, each with a toy: a child with a ball, a puppy with a stick, a crow on a sloping roof, an octopus with a floating bottle, and a bumblebee beside a tiny wooden ball, with a question mark above the bee.
explanations.context: This card says honestly that 'play' has no exact scientific definition, and shows the working tests scientists use instead.

explanations.concept: Why do animals, including us, play at all? Nobody is sure
explanations.definition: Play uses up energy and can lead to injuries, yet young animals of many kinds do it every day. Scientists have several ideas about why, and no single one is accepted.
explanations.description: A playing puppy burns food and may get hurt. A playing fawn makes noise that a leopard could hear. If play gave nothing back, animals who played less would do better. Yet play is found all over the animal world. So scientists think play must give something important. Here science runs out. There are at least four ideas about what play gives. It may be practice for grown-up skills. It may be training for surprises, such as slipping or being knocked over. It may be needed for the growing brain to learn how to get along with others. Or play may simply feel good, with no further purpose needed, as music does. More than one of these could be true at once. Which idea would you test first, and how?
examples: A kitten who stalks a ball of wool uses the same moves that a grown cat uses to hunt.
Playing lambs and puppies twist and tumble on purpose, and put themselves off balance.
Grown-up dogs, otters, crows and people go on playing, long after they have learned their grown-up skills.

perspectives.who: Karl Groos, a German thinker, in 'The Play of Animals', published in German in 1896
perspectives.explanation: He said play is practice. Young animals rehearse hunting, fleeing and fighting while mistakes are still cheap. Against this, kittens who play more have not been shown to become better hunters.

perspectives.who: Marek Špinka, Ruth Newberry and Marc Bekoff, in a paper of 2001
perspectives.explanation: They said play is training for the unexpected. Animals at play throw themselves off balance and give up control on purpose. This may teach the body and the feelings to recover quickly when something goes wrong.

perspectives.who: Sergio Pellis and Vivien Pellis, who study rats in Canada
perspectives.explanation: Young rats who grow up with no chance to play-wrestle with other young rats handle later meetings with strangers badly. The front part of their brain also develops differently. The Pellises think play with others tunes the brain for social life.

perspectives.who: Jaak Panksepp, who found the chirps of tickled rats in the late 1990s
perspectives.explanation: He held that the joy of play is built into old, deep parts of the brain that mammals share. For him the first answer to 'why play?' is that it feels good. Whatever it is useful for comes on top of that.

explanations.art: A puppy tumbling head over heels on grass, with four thought-bubbles above showing a hunting dog, a dog slipping and recovering, two dogs greeting, and a smiling face.
explanations.context: This card gives the main ideas about why play exists, and says plainly that the question is not settled.

agreed.text: Children who spend more time outdoors in daylight are less likely to become short-sighted, which means needing glasses to see far things clearly.
agreed.evidence: In Guangzhou, China, Mingguang He and his team added one 40-minute outdoor class to every school day in six schools, for about 950 children aged six and seven. Six other schools carried on as before. After three years, about 30 in 100 children in the outdoor schools had become short-sighted, against about 40 in 100 in the other schools. The study was published in 2015. Scientists think bright daylight is what helps the growing eye.

agreed.text: Many children's games are hundreds of years old and have been passed from child to child with little change.
agreed.evidence: In 1560 the painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted 'Children's Games', which hangs in a museum in Vienna. It shows more than 200 children playing about 80 games. Many can still be recognised today: leapfrog, blind man's buff, rolling a hoop, spinning tops, walking on stilts and a game like five stones.

agreed.text: A game does not need a prize of food or money. Play can be its own reward, for rats as well as for people.
agreed.evidence: In the hide-and-seek study of 2019, Annika Reinhold and her team never paid the rats with food. A rat who found the hidden person was tickled and played with. That was enough for the rats to learn the game and to keep playing it. Some rats, once found, ran off and hid again, which made the game last longer and put off the tickle.

challenging.claim: Play-fighting should be stopped, because it turns into real fighting.
challenging.who: A common view among teachers and parents, tested by Anthony Pellegrini in American primary schools in 1988 and by Peter Smith in Britain
challenging.for: Play-fighting looks like fighting, and children do sometimes get hurt or upset. A grown-up in charge of forty children cannot watch every pair, so a simple ban feels safest.
challenging.against: Pellegrini watched playgrounds and counted. For most children, play-fighting turned into a real fight only about 1 time in 100. Children who play-fought were smiling, took turns at being on top, and stayed together afterwards. For children whom classmates tended to leave out, it turned real more often. So the same play is safe for most pairs and needs watching for a few.
challenging.context: Grown-ups often stop rough play. This asks what careful watching of playgrounds found, and where the worry is still fair.

challenging.claim: Competitive games make children less kind, so children should mostly play cooperative games.
challenging.who: Alfie Kohn, an American writer, in 'No Contest: The Case Against Competition', 1986, drawing on Terry Orlick's studies
challenging.for: When only one can win, the other players stand between you and the prize. Orlick found that five-year-olds shared more after weeks of cooperative games. Kohn collected studies in which children learned and created better when they were not competing.
challenging.against: Many of those studies were small and short. Tauer and Harackiewicz found in 2004 that children enjoyed a task most when a team cooperated inside and competed outside. Many players say a hard, fair contest with a friend makes the friendship stronger. Rats and dogs compete in play and stay friends, as long as each side sometimes wins.
challenging.context: Some people think games with winners teach selfishness. This gives the evidence for that worry and the evidence against it.

challenging.claim: Babies already expect fairness, long before anyone teaches them to share.
challenging.who: Marco Schmidt and Jessica Sommerville in 2011, and Stephanie Sloane, Renée Baillargeon and David Premack in 2012
challenging.for: Babies look longer at things that surprise them. Babies of 15 months looked longer when a grown-up gave two people unequal amounts of biscuits than when the amounts were equal. Babies of 19 months did the same with toys. This suggests they expected equal shares.
challenging.against: Looking for longer can have many causes, and some looking-time results have been hard to repeat. When children of three and four actually share out sweets, most keep more for themselves, as Fehr's team found in 2008. So expecting fairness from others and being fair yourself may be two separate things that grow at different times.
challenging.context: Is the feeling for fairness something we are born with, or something we learn? This gives a claim from tests with babies and the doubts about it.

challenging.claim: Children today play freely far less than children used to, and this is harming their minds.
challenging.who: Peter Gray, an American psychologist, in 'The Decline of Play and the Rise of Psychopathology in Children and Adolescents', 2011
challenging.for: In the United States, the hours children spend playing freely with other children, with no grown-up in charge, fell over about fifty years. Over the same years, measures of worry and sadness in young people rose. Gray argues that free play is where children learn to make rules, settle quarrels and face small fears.
challenging.against: Two things changing over the same years does not show that one caused the other. Many other things changed in those years too. Most of the numbers come from one country. The Opies noted in 1969 that grown-ups in every age have said children's games are dying, and yet they found the games alive on every street. Nobody has measured this carefully for children in India.
challenging.context: A well-known claim says that less free play is making children unhappy. It is here because it matters to every family, and because the proof is not yet strong.

big_questions.q: You break a rule when nobody is looking, and you finish first. Did you win the game?
big_questions.hint: Ask what the others were playing, and what you were playing. Were they the same game?

big_questions.q: The seeds are still on the floor, but one player has stopped keeping the rule. Where has the game gone?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the game was before. Was it in the seeds, in one player's head, or somewhere else?

big_questions.q: A big child lets a small child win. Is that kind, or is it a way of not telling the truth?
big_questions.hint: Think about a big dog who rolls over for a puppy. Then think about how the small child would feel on finding out.

big_questions.q: In snakes and ladders the dice makes every move for you. So when you win, what did you do?
big_questions.hint: Compare it with winning at five stones. What part of each win belongs to you?

big_questions.q: Can a rule be a bad rule? How would the players find out?
big_questions.hint: Imagine a rule that says the oldest child always goes first. Ask each player how it feels from their place.

big_questions.q: A child of six and a child of ten run a race. Is it fairer to start at the same line or to give a head start?
big_questions.hint: Try to say what the race is for. Then see if your answer changes.

big_questions.q: A bee rolls a ball and a puppy chases a leaf. How could we ever find out if they are having fun?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you can tell that a friend is having fun, without the friend saying so.

big_questions.q: Can you play a game against yourself? If you can, who loses?
big_questions.hint: Try the ten-seed game with your left hand against your right hand. Notice what is missing, if anything.

big_questions.q: Homes, roads and schools have rules too. Are those rules like game rules, which the players agreed to?
big_questions.hint: Pick one rule you live by, such as stopping at a red light. Ask who made it, who agreed to it, and what happens if nobody keeps it.

open_questions.why_open: There are at least four ideas: practice for grown-up life, training for surprises, tuning the growing brain for life with others, and plain enjoyment. Each fits some findings and fails others. Testing them is hard, because scientists cannot easily stop an animal from playing without changing many other things in that animal's life.

Play is clear in mammals and birds. It has been reported in turtles, fish, octopuses and bumblebees. The answer depends on the definition of play, and there is no agreed one. Nobody has found a way to ask whether beings with very different bodies, such as plants or microbes, do anything that deserves the name.

open_questions.q: Do other animals have a sense of fairness?
open_questions.why_open: Capuchin monkeys and dogs protest in some tests when a partner is paid better. Other teams, using other animals or slightly different tests, did not find it. The tests cannot yet separate 'I got less than her' from 'I got less than I hoped for'.

open_questions.q: Why do children in some places give up an unfairly big share, while children in other places do not?
open_questions.why_open: The seven-country study of 2015 found the difference but could not explain it. It may come from how families share, from schooling, from how people trade, or from something not yet thought of. More places need to be studied, including many more in India.

open_questions.q: How much risk in play is the right amount?
open_questions.why_open: Studies suggest that some risky play helps children judge danger and stay active. Hospital records show that falls cause real harm. No study has yet followed enough children for enough years to say where the best balance lies, and it may differ from child to child.

story.title: The Girl Who Won Every Round
story.note: A made-up story set in Thanjavur, Tamil Nadu. The children, the neighbour and the dogs are imagined, and so is the two-hands rule. What is real: five stones is played as described, its rules differ from place to place, and dogs who play with a much smaller dog often hold back and roll over, as Marc Bekoff and others have filmed. Whether a win that was made easier is a 'real' win is a question people answer differently.
text: It was the May holidays in Thanjavur, and the veranda floor was the only cool place in the house. Ponni, who was seven, sat there with five smooth stones from the river. Across from her sat Anbu, the boy from next door, who was five.
'I will teach you anjukal,' said Ponni. 'Five stones. Throw one up. Pick one from the floor. Catch the first one before it lands. Same hand.'
She showed him. Up, pick, catch. Up, pick, catch. Her hand moved like a bird pecking.
Anbu tried. The stone went up. His small hand closed on a stone on the floor. The first stone hit his wrist and skidded under the bench.
'My turn,' said Ponni. She did all four pick-ups without a miss. 'I win.'
They played again. She won. They played again. She won. By the sixth round Anbu was not looking at the stones any more. He was looking at the gate.
'I win again!' said Ponni.
'I am going home,' said Anbu, and he went.

Ponni played alone. Up, pick, catch. She did a perfect round. Nobody said anything. She did another perfect round. It felt like eating plain rice with no sambar. She had the stones. She had the veranda. She had won six times. So why did it feel as if she had nothing?

In the lane, something was going on. Karuppi, the big black dog who slept under the neem tree, was facing her puppy. The puppy was the size of a coconut. Karuppi dropped her front legs flat on the ground and stuck her tail in the air. The puppy did the same. Then he charged.

Karuppi could have rolled him over with one paw. Ponni had seen her chase a full-grown goat. But Karuppi flopped onto her back. The puppy climbed onto her chest, growling a tiny growl, and chewed her ear. Karuppi wriggled and let him. Then she flipped him gently, and he was underneath. Then she flopped again.
'She keeps losing on purpose,' said Ponni.
'Does she?' said Zubeida aunty. She was sitting on the next step, threading jasmine. 'It looks to me as if she is keeping the game going. If she played with all her strength, how long would he stay?'
Ponni thought of Anbu looking at the gate.
'But in anjukal the rule is one hand,' she said. 'That is the real rule.'
'In my village near Nagapattinam,' said Zubeida aunty, 'little ones caught with two hands until their hands grew. Who told you one hand was the real rule?'
'My cousin.'
'And who told her?'
Ponni did not know. She picked up the stones and went next door.
'New rule,' she told Anbu. 'You may catch with two hands. I must use one. Do you agree?'
Anbu frowned. 'That is cheating.'
Ponni thought about it. 'Cheating is when one person changes the rule and hides it. We are both saying it aloud. So it is a rule.'
They played on Anbu's step. In the third round Ponni's stone clipped her thumb and fell. Anbu, with his tongue between his teeth, did all four pick-ups.
'I WON!' His shout sent the crows off the wall.

Something hot went through Ponni's chest. She did not like it. Then she noticed that she was already leaning forward, and her hand was already reaching for the stones. She wanted the next round more than she had wanted any round all morning.
They played until the lamps were lit. Ponni won most rounds. Anbu won some. Karuppi slept under the neem tree with the puppy on top of her.
As he gathered the stones, Anbu asked, 'When my hands are big, will we go back to one hand?'
'We will decide then,' said Ponni.
He was quiet for a bit. Then he asked the harder thing. 'Ponni akka. Did I really win? Or did you make it easy?'
Ponni looked at Karuppi, and at the puppy rising and falling on her breath. She opened her mouth to answer. Then she closed it again, because she did not know.
story.epiphany: Ponni won every round and ended up with five stones and no game. A game needs a second player who has a real chance, so the stronger player has a reason to change something. Karuppi changed how hard she played. Ponni changed a rule aloud, with Anbu's agreement.
ask: Anbu asked if he had really won. What would you tell him?
Karuppi rolled over for her puppy. Was she pretending, playing or teaching? How could you find out?
Zubeida aunty's village and Ponni's street had different rules for the same game. Is one of them the real rule?
Ponni felt something hot in her chest when she lost, and then she wanted to play again. Have you felt both of those together?

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many thinkers held that play was only spare energy spilling out. Herbert Spencer, an English thinker, wrote this in 1855. It fitted what people saw: well-fed young animals played, and tired or hungry ones did not. In 1896 Karl Groos argued that play must be useful, or animals would not spend so much effort on it. But the idea that play was shapeless fooling about stayed. From the 1970s, Marc Bekoff filmed dogs, wolves and coyotes at play and studied the films a fraction of a second at a time. He found order: the bow before the chase, the gentle bite, the swap of who is on top. In the late 1990s, Jaak Panksepp and Jeffrey Burgdorf tickled rats and recorded chirps too high for human ears. The rats ran back to the hand for more. In 2019, Annika Reinhold's team played hide and seek with rats. In 2022, Samadi Galpayage Dona filmed bumblebees rolling balls. Step by step, play turned out to be widespread, orderly and wanted for its own sake.
how_we_found_out.who: Herbert Spencer, Karl Groos, Marc Bekoff, Jaak Panksepp, Jeffrey Burgdorf, Annika Reinhold, Samadi Galpayage Dona
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People once thought play was leftover energy with no order and no purpose, and that only humans had games with rules. It was believable because only well-fed young animals seemed to play, and because the rules of animal play are too quick to see without slowed-down film.

roots.context: We have been learning what makes a game: rules, turns, fairness and a second player. Now we ask what a game tells us about ourselves, about life and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Two Ways Test, you played with ten seeds, first with a rule and then with no rule. The seeds, the floor and the two players were the same both times. With the rule there was a game. Without the rule there was only grabbing. So the game was made by the two of you together, and that includes the player who was trying to beat you.
deep_truth.habit: We call the other player 'against me'. That label makes a game look like two separate sides, each wanting the other gone. The test shows that the other side is half of what makes the game exist.
deep_truth.evidence: With the turn rule, the ten-seed game had a start, an end and a winner that both players accepted. In the round with no rule, the same ten seeds were gone in a few seconds, and the players could not agree on who had won.

three.who_am_i: In a game you say 'my side'. But you are also holding the rule, and the rule belongs to both sides. So there is more to you than your side. Part of you is already looking after the whole game.
three.what_is_life: Puppies, young rats, crows and children all play, and nobody has to make them. A big dog makes herself small so that a little one can join in. Wherever life plays, the stronger and the weaker find a way to stay together.
three.what_is_this_world: A game is a small world with its own place, its own time and its own rules. The big world also follows patterns, such as things falling down and day following night. Nobody agreed to those. Science can describe them, and cannot yet say why the world has them.

roots.thread: Take away the second player and the game is gone, though every seed is still there. So a game never belongs to one player. It exists between the players, in what they keep together. The same is true of a conversation, a friendship and a song sung in turns. Consciousness is the ground that every player arises from, and in a game the two sides are that one ground playing with itself. Many scientists do not take this last step, and their view is given below.

teachings.teaching: The verse says that creation is 'lila', which means play, as we see play in the world. The teacher Shankara explains it this way: a king who has everything still plays, with no need behind it. In the same way, he says, the world comes out of the One with no need behind it, as play.
teachings.link: This is a teaching and not a finding. The lesson's science meets it at one point: rats and people play with no prize, for the play itself. The sages said the same of the whole world. Science has not tested that and may not be able to.

teachings.teaching: Treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat as alike, and then act.
teachings.link: In the ten-seed game, the winner and the loser made the game together, and next round they may swap. Seen from the side of the whole game, winning and losing are two parts of one thing.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, a Greek thinker of about 500 BCE, fragment 52 in the Diels-Kranz numbering
teachings.teaching: He wrote that time is a child playing, moving pieces on a board, and that the kingdom belongs to the child.
teachings.link: A thinker far from India also reached for a game to describe the world. He left only this one line about it, so nobody knows exactly what he meant. It can be read as saying that the world's order is like a game's order: real, and held with a light hand.

science.text: Animals who play together hold back their strength, signal before rough moves and take turns at being on top. This has been filmed and counted in dogs, wolves, coyotes and rats.
Whether insects, fish and octopuses feel anything like fun when they do things that pass the tests for play is not known.

other_view.view: They say play, rules and fairness need no explanation beyond living bodies. Animals who lived in groups did better when they could play without hurting each other, so signals and holding back were passed on from parents to young. The feeling that a game is 'between us' is something each brain makes separately. Charvaka thinkers of ancient India would have agreed that nothing beyond the body is needed.

practice.title: One seed, two hands
practice.say: Sit facing your child, knees almost touching. Say: 'We have one seed. I will put it in your hand while I breathe out. Then you wait for one whole breath. Then you put it in my hand while you breathe out.' Pass the seed back and forth like this, slowly, about ten times, without talking. Then ask: 'What was it like when the seed was in your hand? What was it like when your hand was empty and waiting?'
practice.kid: Sit facing someone. Hold one seed. Breathe out and put it in their hand. Wait for one whole breath with your hand empty. They breathe out and give it back. Do this ten times without talking. Notice how giving feels, and how waiting feels.

ask: When you play against a friend, are the two of you doing two things or one thing?
The player who beat you also helped to make the game. Does knowing that change how losing feels?
A game's rules were agreed by its players. Who, if anyone, agreed to the patterns the whole world follows?

playtest: The deep part and the routine parts are written from reading. Nothing has been tried at home with a child. Before publishing, play the Two Ways Test (e1) with a parent and a child and with two children.
