terms.meaning: A game is play with rules that all the players agree to keep.
terms.example: Hide and seek is a game. The seeker counts to twenty, and the others hide.
terms.art: Two children sitting on a veranda floor with a small heap of seeds between them, both pointing at the heap.

terms.meaning: A rule is a sentence that says what players may do, must do or must not do.
terms.example: In ludo, the rule says you move your token as many squares as the dice shows.
terms.art: A child holding up three fingers while a friend nods, with a ludo board on the floor.

terms.meaning: A goal is what the players are trying to do in a game.
terms.example: In hide and seek, the seeker's goal is to find everyone. The goal of the hiders is to stay hidden.
terms.art: A girl with her eyes covered counting, and three children crouching behind a water drum.

terms.meaning: A turn is your go. One player acts while the others wait. Then the next player acts.
terms.example: In carrom, you flick the striker on your turn. Then the next player flicks it.
terms.art: Two children on either side of a carrom board, one flicking the striker and one waiting with hands in her lap.

terms.meaning: To cheat is to break a rule in secret while the other players keep it.
terms.example: A girl rolls a three at ludo, but she moves her token four squares when nobody is looking.
terms.art: A girl at a ludo board quietly sliding her token one square too far while two friends look away.

terms.meaning: A mistake is breaking a rule by accident. It is not done on purpose and not hidden.
terms.example: A boy flicks the carrom striker when it is not his turn. He says sorry, and they put the coin back.
terms.art: A boy with his hand over his mouth, a carrom striker in the middle of the board and his friend smiling.

terms.meaning: An indoor game is a game you can play inside a room.
terms.example: Carrom, ludo, chess and five stones are indoor games. Rain does not stop them.
terms.art: A family on a mat around a carrom board with rain falling outside the window.

terms.meaning: An outdoor game is a game that needs open space, such as a lane, a courtyard, a terrace or a playground.
terms.example: Kho-kho, kabaddi and cricket are outdoor games. You run, jump and dodge.
terms.art: Children running in a courtyard in the evening light, one with a ball and two chasing.

terms.meaning: Hopscotch is a game where you hop through squares drawn on the ground. It has many names across India.
terms.example: It is nondi or paandi in Tamil Nadu, kunte bille in Karnataka and ekka dokka in Bengal.
terms.art: A girl hopping on one foot through chalk squares numbered one to six on a lane.

terms.meaning: Chaturanga is an old game from India, played by about the 6th century CE. Chess grew from it.
terms.example: Chaturanga had foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots, like the pieces in chess.
terms.art: An old wooden board with carved elephants, horses and foot soldiers, and two players leaning over it.

terms.meaning: A dice is a small cube with dots on its faces. You roll it, and the top face tells you the number.
terms.example: In snakes and ladders, the dice shows 4, so you move your token four squares.
terms.art: A hand rolling a white dice across a board, with the dice caught in the middle of a tumble.

terms.meaning: Luck is what happens by chance, and not by your choice.
terms.example: You roll a six on the dice. You did not choose it, so that was luck.
terms.art: A child with her mouth open as a dice lands showing six.

terms.meaning: Skill is what you get better at by practising.
terms.example: The more you practise flicking the carrom striker, the more coins you pocket. That is skill.
terms.art: A boy lining up a carrom flick with one eye closed, his tongue between his teeth.

terms.meaning: A promise is when someone says they will do something, and then does it, so others can trust them.
terms.example: A grown-up says, 'You can play after dinner.' After dinner, the child plays. The promise was kept.
terms.art: A grown-up and a child shaking little fingers in a kitchen doorway.

terms.meaning: A game or a sharing is fair when no player is treated worse than another without a good reason. People do not agree on one meaning of fair.
terms.example: Each child gets two laddus. Some children say that is fair. Others say the child who missed lunch should get more.
terms.art: Two children each holding two laddus on a steel plate, with a third child looking at the plate.

terms.meaning: A head start is when one player starts a race closer to the finish line, or starts earlier.
terms.example: A big child lets a small child start five steps ahead in a race to the gate.
terms.art: A small child standing five steps ahead of a big child on a lane, both facing a gate.

terms.meaning: To share is to give each person a part of something, so that everyone has some.
terms.example: Six laddus shared between two children is three laddus each.
terms.art: Six laddus on a plate, with two children each holding three.

terms.meaning: To win is to reach the goal of the game before the others, or to do better than the others.
terms.example: In the ten-seed game, you win by taking the last seed.
terms.art: A child with both arms raised and a friend clapping beside her.

terms.meaning: To lose is not to reach the goal first. A player who loses has still helped to make the game.
terms.example: You lose at hide and seek when the seeker finds you. Then you can seek next time.
terms.art: A boy found behind a door, laughing, with the seeker pointing at him.

terms.meaning: In a competitive game, the players try to beat each other.
terms.example: In a race to the gate, each runner tries to get there first.
terms.art: Four children racing along a lane towards a gate, one just ahead.

terms.meaning: In a cooperative game, all the players are on one side. They win together or lose together.
terms.example: Two friends keep a balloon in the air. If the balloon touches the floor, both of them lose.
terms.art: Two children laughing, both with hands up, with a red balloon between them.

terms.meaning: A safety rule is a rule that keeps players from getting hurt.
terms.example: In a running game, you touch and you never push. This protects backs and wrists.
terms.art: Two children chasing each other on a dry terrace, the chaser gently touching the other's shoulder.

terms.meaning: A stop word is a word that all the players agree means 'stop now'. When anyone says it, everyone stops.
terms.example: Before a chasing game, the children agree that the word is 'Stop'. A child trips and calls it, and the game stops.
terms.art: A child with her hand up and her mouth open saying Stop, and three children frozen in the middle of running.

terms.meaning: A risk is a small danger that a child can see and choose to take.
terms.example: Jumping from the second step is a risk. A child can look at the height and decide.
terms.art: A child on the bottom step of a staircase looking down at the floor, one foot ready to jump.

terms.meaning: A hazard is a danger that a child cannot see.
terms.example: A wet patch under a rug is a hazard. The child does not know it is there.
terms.art: A rug in a hallway with a shining puddle under one corner, and a child's bare foot about to step on it.

terms.meaning: Play is doing something for the fun of doing it. Scientists have no final agreed meaning of play.
terms.example: Two puppies chase each other round a neem tree. Nobody gives them a prize.
terms.art: Two puppies tumbling in the dust under a neem tree.

terms.meaning: Energy is what lets you run, jump and grow, and it comes from your food. Physicists can calculate energy and it works, but nobody has a final answer to what energy is.
terms.example: After a long game of tag, you feel hungry. Your body used up energy, and a meal gives you more.
terms.art: A tired child eating a plate of rice and dal after a game in the lane.

terms.meaning: A play bow is when a dog lowers her front legs flat and keeps her back end up in the air. It is a signal that means 'This is play'.
terms.example: Before a chase, one street dog does a play bow. The other dog bows back, and they dash off.
terms.art: A street dog in a play bow, front legs flat on the ground and tail high in the air, facing a smaller dog.

terms.meaning: A signal is a sign that tells others something.
terms.example: A dog's play bow says, 'I am not attacking.' A traffic light is a signal too.
terms.art: A dog in a play bow on the left and a red traffic light on the right.

terms.meaning: Short-sighted means you see near things clearly, but far things look blurred. Glasses can help.
terms.example: A short-sighted child sees her book clearly, but she cannot read the board across the room.
terms.art: A child squinting at a blackboard far away, with a book held close in her hand.

terms.meaning: A definition is a sentence that says exactly what a word means. For some words, such as play, scientists have no agreed one.
terms.example: A dictionary gives a definition of 'rule'. For 'play', scientists use five working tests instead.
terms.art: An open dictionary with a magnifying glass over one word.

games.title: Fair, Not Fair, or It Depends?
games.context: This is a card game. Each card describes a moment in a game. Players show a token and give a reason.

items.f: Two children take turns on a swing. Each gets ten pushes.
items.b: YES, fair. Both get the same number of pushes.

items.f: A big child and a baby run a race from the same line.
items.b: IT DEPENDS. The same line is the same for both. But the baby is much smaller. Talk about what the race is for.

items.f: The oldest child always goes first in every game.
items.b: IT DEPENDS. Some children say it is fair, because it is a rule. Others say turns should change round the circle.

items.f: Nobody tells a new girl the rules, and then she loses.
items.b: NO. All the players must know the rules before they start.

items.f: A child peeps during the counting in hide and seek.
items.b: NO. That is cheating. The others are keeping the rule and she is not.

items.f: A child who missed lunch gets an extra laddu.
items.b: IT DEPENDS. Some say more for who needs more is fair. Some say the same for everyone is fair.

items.f: Before the game, everyone agrees the youngest child gets a two-step head start.
items.b: YES. Everyone agreed first, so the rule is shared.

items.f: A big child lets a small child win without telling her.
items.b: IT DEPENDS. It can be kind. But the small child may feel cheated when she finds out.

items.f: In snakes and ladders, one player rolls many sixes by chance.
items.b: YES. Every player has the same chance on every roll, so the dice is fair, even if it feels unlucky.

items.f: Halfway through, one player changes a rule in secret so that she wins.
items.b: NO. A rule can change only when everybody agrees.

items.f: Before round two, all the players agree to change one rule.
items.b: YES. A rule can change when everyone agrees to the change.

items.f: The player who loses is told she may never play again.
items.b: NO. The game needs the player who lost, and she can play again next round.

printables.title: 12 answer tokens: 3 for each of up to 4 players

rules: Cut out the 12 cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
Cut out the tokens. Each player takes one of each kind: YES, NO and IT DEPENDS. Players who are fewer than four put the extra tokens away.
One player reads the top card aloud. Everyone puts one token face down, then turns it over at the same time.
Each player says one reason for the token. A player who gives a reason scores one point, even if the others disagree.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud. Players may change their mind. Then the next player reads the next card.
The game ends when all 12 cards are read. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, count your reasons and try to beat your last total.

setup.art: Three children and a grown-up in a ring on a floor, each with three tokens, a card being read aloud.
setup.caption: 1. Read a card. Everyone puts down a token.

setup.art: Four tokens turned over at once, two YES, one NO and one IT DEPENDS, and a child talking with her hands.
setup.caption: 2. Turn them over and say why.

flow.do: Read the rules aloud. Show the three tokens. Explain that IT DEPENDS is a real answer, and that the reason matters more than the token.
flow.say: Here are the three tokens. YES means fair. NO means not fair. IT DEPENDS means it could go either way. Every player gives a reason.
flow.kid: Look at the three tokens. Each one is a real answer. Give a reason with each.

flow.do: Play all 12 cards. After each card, count down 'one, two, three' and show the tokens. Ask each player for a reason. Then read the back.
flow.say: Here is the card. Put down your token. One, two, three. Show! Now, why did you choose that one?
flow.kid: Read the card. Put down your token. Turn it over. Say why.

ask.q: Why did you choose that token?
good: Everyone gets the same.
The rule was agreed before.
It depends on who needs more.

flow.parent: Do not mark a token right on an IT DEPENDS card. Ask each player for a reason and let them disagree. Three of the cards are plain NO or YES, to give some firm ground.

flow.do: Count the points. Ask which card the players disagreed about most, and what would help them to agree.
flow.say: Count your points. Which card did we disagree about most? What would help us agree?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card did you disagree about most?

ask.q: What would help players agree about a card?
good: Ask what the game is for.
Agree the rule before the game starts.

games.title: Snakes and Ladders: Luck First, Then a Choice
games.context: This is a small snakes and ladders game on a board of twenty squares. You play it once by luck, and once with a choice.

printables.title: 2 player tokens
items: Player 1 token: a bean or a button
Player 2 token: a different bean or button

rules: Draw the 20 squares in a snaking row on a sheet of paper, or write them on 20 small papers. Number them 1 to 20. Mark the ladders and snakes shown.
Put the six number slips in a bowl. On your turn, draw a slip without looking, read the number, and put it back.
Move your token that many squares. If you land on the bottom of a ladder, go up. If you land on a snake, slide down.
You win when you land on square 20 or go past it.
Game one has no choices. The slip decides every move. Play it once.
In game two, after you draw a slip you may move that number or one square fewer. Play it once.
Both players go on until someone wins. Then talk about which game had more choices.

setup.art: A hand-drawn board of twenty squares with two ladders and two snakes, two bean tokens on square one and a bowl of numbered slips.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the board. Put the slips in a bowl.

setup.art: Two children each holding a bean token, with one drawing a slip from the bowl and the other watching the board.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a slip. Move your token.

flow.do: Draw the board, mark the ladders and snakes, and put the slips in the bowl. Each player puts a token on square 1.
flow.say: Here is our board. Squares three and six have ladders. Squares seventeen and nineteen have snakes. Pick your tokens and put them on one.
flow.kid: Look at the board. Put your token on square one.

flow.do: Play game one, using the slips only. Do not give any choices. Say the number aloud each turn.
flow.say: Draw a slip. Move that many squares. Whoever gets to twenty first wins.
flow.kid: Draw a slip. Move your token. Reach twenty to win.

ask.q: In this game, what choices did you make?
good: None, the slip decided.
I only moved the token.

flow.do: Play game two. After each draw, the player may move the number or one fewer. Then ask which game was luck, and which game had some skill.
flow.say: Now, after you draw, you may move that number or one fewer. Who will win this time?
flow.kid: Play again. You may move the number or one fewer. Is it still luck?

ask.q: Which game had more skill in it, and why?
good: The second one, because we could choose.
The first was only luck.

flow.parent: Neither game is a game of skill. The second only lets a child make a choice. A choice is where skill begins.

experiments.title: The Two Ways Test: ten seeds, with a rule and with no rule
experiments.context: In this test you play with ten seeds two ways, first with a turn rule and then with no rule at all. You find out what the rule does.
experiments.question: Are ten seeds a game when there is a rule? Are they a game when there is no rule?
experiments.predict: Before you play, guess what will happen in the round with no rule. How long will it last? Will you both want to play again? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Both ways use the same ten seeds, the same floor and the same two players. Only the rule changes. We play the rule round three times, because one try can be a fluke. Who goes first swaps each time, so nobody always gets the first go. The no-rule round is over in seconds, so we play it once. You may play it again if you like.
results_table: How long did it last? (a few seconds, half a minute, a minute or more)
Did you both agree who won? (yes or no)
Did you both want to play again? (yes or no)

materials.item: 10 tamarind seeds, or 10 dried beans, or 10 buttons of one kind
a clean mat or a patch of floor
a small bowl to keep the seeds in
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: The seeds are small, so keep them away from children under five. Count all ten back into the bowl at the end. Call the stop word at once if hands get rough.

schedule.what: Guess, play the rule round three times, play the no-rule round once, and fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with one line for each round. Then draw the rule round and the no-rule round, one picture each.

setup.art: Ten tamarind seeds in a heap on a mat, a child sitting on one side and a grown-up on the other, with a small bowl between them.
setup.caption: 1. Ten seeds, two players and a stop word.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up taking turns, each holding up one finger or two fingers, with the seeds in a row between them.
setup.caption: 2. Round with a rule: take one seed or two seeds on your turn. Whoever takes the last seed wins.

setup.art: Two pairs of hands grabbing at a heap of seeds at the same moment, seeds flying, and a grown-up holding up a hand to say stop.
setup.caption: 3. Round with no rule: just get seeds. If it gets rough, say the stop word.

flow.do: Sit on the floor facing your child. Put ten seeds in a heap between you. Choose a stop word together, such as 'Stop'. Say that anyone may call it at any time, and then all hands go back.
flow.say: We have ten seeds and two players. We will play two ways. If anyone says the stop word, all hands go back at once.
flow.kid: Sit facing your partner. Put ten seeds in a heap. Pick a stop word, such as 'Stop'.
flow.parent: Do this only with children over five at the table, because the seeds are small. Count all ten back at the end.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before anything is played. Write the guess on the paper. Do not correct it.
flow.say: Soon we will play a round with no rule at all. We will only say 'get seeds'. What do you think will happen? How long will it last? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what will happen when there is no rule. Say why you think so.

ask.q: What will happen in the round with no rule, and why do you think so?
good: We will grab, and it will be over fast.
Nobody will know what to do.
It will be fun, because we can take lots.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. A guess that turns out wrong is useful, because the test answers it.

flow.do: Say the rule aloud: 'We take turns. On your turn, take one seed or two seeds. Whoever takes the last seed wins.' Your child goes first. Play. Then play two more rounds. Swap who goes first each time. After each round, ask who won, and write how long it took.
flow.say: On your turn, take one seed or two seeds. Whoever takes the last seed wins. Who won? Do we agree? Shall we play again?
flow.kid: Take turns. Take one seed or two seeds. Whoever takes the last seed wins. Play three times.

ask.q: How did you know who won?
good: Whoever took the last seed won.
We both saw the last seed go.

flow.parent: Each round takes about a minute. Let the winner be the winner, and let the other player feel it. Do not hint at the pattern in the game. Your child may find it alone.

flow.do: Put all ten seeds back in a heap. Say: 'This round has no rule. Get seeds.' Then say 'Go.' Both players get seeds. Say 'Stop' when the seeds are gone. Do not add any rule. If hands get rough, call the stop word.
flow.say: This round has no rule at all. Just get seeds. Ready? Go!
flow.kid: Put ten seeds in a heap. When your grown-up says go, get seeds. Say the stop word if it gets rough.
flow.parent: This round is over in a few seconds. Do not explain and do not add rules. Whatever happens, ask the same questions as before.

flow.do: Ask the same questions as after each rule round. Then fill in the table together, with one line for each round.
flow.say: In this round, who won? Do we agree? Do we want to play it again?
flow.kid: Fill in your table. Write who won, and write whether you want to play again.

ask.q: In the round with no rule, who won?
good: I did, because I got more.
Nobody, because we never said what winning was.
We do not agree.

flow.parent: If you both agree who won in the no-rule round, that is a real result. Ask what 'win' meant, since nobody said so before you started.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask what was different between the two ways. The seeds, the floor and the two of you were the same both times.
flow.say: The seeds were the same. The floor was the same. We were the same. What was different? Where did the game come from?
flow.kid: Look at your table. What was different between the two ways?

check.q: The seeds were the same both times. What made the first way a game?
options: The seeds had a rule on them
Both players agreed to keep a rule
check.why: Nothing on the floor changed. The game came from what both players agreed to keep.

flow.parent: Wait for your child's own words first. Then say it plainly: with the rule you had a game, and without the rule you had grabbing. A game needs the rule and also a second player who keeps it.

experiments.think: Could you play the ten-seed game with only one player? Who would you play against?

activities.title: Same Seeds, Different Game
activities.context: In this activity you play two games with the same ten seeds. Then you change one rule and see what happens.

materials.item: 10 tamarind seeds or dried beans
a small bowl
a strip of tape or a rolled sock to mark a line

schedule.what: Play odd or even, then the bowl toss, then change one rule.

activities.record: Draw the two games. Under each, write the rule in one sentence.

setup.art: A child holding a closed fist over a heap of seeds while a grown-up looks at the fist and thinks.
setup.caption: 1. Odd or even: how many seeds are in the fist?

setup.art: A child standing behind a tape line tossing a seed into a steel bowl one big step away.
setup.caption: 2. Bowl toss: toss five seeds from the line.

flow.do: Hold some seeds in your closed fist, more than zero and fewer than ten. Your child guesses 'odd' or 'even'. Open your fist and count together. If the guess is right, your child gets a point. Swap roles.
flow.say: Hide some seeds in your fist. I will guess odd or even. Then we open your fist and count.
flow.kid: Hide some seeds in your fist. Your partner guesses odd or even. Open your hand and count.

ask.q: What is the rule of this game?
good: Guess odd or even. If you are right, you get a point.

flow.do: Put the bowl on the floor. Make a line one big step back with tape or a rolled sock. Toss five seeds, one at a time, into the bowl. Count how many land inside. Swap.
flow.say: Stand behind the line. Toss five seeds into the bowl, one at a time. Count the ones that go in.
flow.kid: Stand behind the line. Toss five seeds into the bowl. Count the seeds that go in.
flow.parent: Seeds that bounce out are not counted. Let your child have a second go at five if they like.

flow.do: Ask what was the same in both games and what was different. Then change one rule of odd or even, for example guess a number from one to five. Say the new rule aloud, then play one round.
flow.say: Both games used the same ten seeds. What was different? Now let us change one rule of odd or even. Say the new rule aloud before we start.
flow.kid: The seeds were the same in both games. What changed? Now change one rule and play.

ask.q: The seeds were the same. So what made two different games?
good: The rule.
What we agreed to do with the seeds.

activities.think: What is a third game you could play with the same ten seeds? Say its rule in one sentence.
activities.safety: Seeds are small. Keep them away from children under five, and count them all back into the bowl.

activities.title: Act It Out: Indoor or Outdoor?
activities.context: In this activity you act out games without speaking, and your partner guesses the game and where it is played.

materials.item: 2 sheets of paper
a pencil

schedule.what: Act out games, guess them, and stand on the sheet where they are played.

activities.record: Write or draw the three games you like best, and mark each INDOOR or OUTDOOR.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper on a floor, one with the word INDOOR and a roof drawn on it, one with the word OUTDOOR and a sun drawn on it.
setup.caption: 1. Two sheets: INDOOR and OUTDOOR.

setup.art: A grown-up miming a flick of a carrom striker while a child shouts the answer and points to the INDOOR sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Act without words. Guess the game. Stand on a sheet.

flow.do: Write INDOOR on one sheet and OUTDOOR on the other. Put them on the floor a few steps apart. Explain that an indoor game fits in a room and an outdoor game needs open space.
flow.say: An indoor game fits in a room. An outdoor game needs open space. I will act out a game with no words. You guess it, and stand on the right sheet.
flow.kid: Look at the two sheets. One is for games inside. One is for games in open space.

flow.do: Act out one game without a word, such as carrom, ludo, chess, kabaddi, kho-kho, cricket or hide and seek. Your child guesses it, stands on a sheet, and says one rule or one thing the game needs. Then swap, and your child acts.
flow.say: Guess my game. Where is it played? Tell me one rule of it.
flow.kid: Guess the game. Stand on the right sheet. Say one rule.

ask.q: Why does that game need a room, or open space?
good: Kho-kho needs space to run.
Carrom fits on a board on a table.

flow.parent: If a game fits both, such as hopscotch with chalk outside or tape inside, let your child stand between the sheets and say what changes.

flow.do: Ask which game would still work if it rained. Ask which games your family has played, and which one your child would like to learn.
flow.say: It starts to rain. Which of the games could we still play? Which game have you never played?
flow.kid: It rains. Which games can you still play? Pick one game you have never played.

ask.q: Which games can you still play when it rains?
good: Carrom, ludo, chess, five stones.
Games that fit in a room.

activities.think: Which game would you like to learn, and who could teach you?

activities.title: Hopscotch Has Many Names
activities.context: In this activity you make a hopscotch row and play it. Then you find out how many names this one game has across India.

materials.item: paper masking tape, or chalk if you play outside
a flat marker, such as a folded cloth or a bottle cap

schedule.what: Make the row of squares, hop through it, then say the game's names.

activities.record: Draw the squares you made, and write one of the game's names under the picture.

setup.art: A strip of masking tape forming a row of six squares on a floor, with numbers one to six written inside them.
setup.caption: 1. Six squares, each as big as a book.

setup.art: A girl hopping on one foot through the squares, with a folded cloth marker lying in square one.
setup.caption: 2. Hop on one foot. Pick up the marker on the way back.

flow.do: Tear tape to make a row of six squares on a dry, flat floor, each about the size of a book. Write the numbers 1 to 6 in them. Or draw them with chalk on the ground outside. Wipe up any water first.
flow.say: We will make a row of six squares. Each is about as big as a book. Please write the numbers one to six inside them.
flow.kid: Help make six squares with tape. Write the numbers one to six in them.
flow.parent: Play only on a dry, flat floor, in chappals or bare feet. Move the furniture away from the row first.

flow.do: Toss the marker into square 1. Hop on one foot over square 1 and through squares 2 to 6. Turn round and hop back. Pick up the marker without putting your other foot down. Then toss to square 2. If you put your other foot down, your turn ends.
flow.say: Throw the marker into square one. Hop on one foot over it and through the rest. Turn, hop back, and pick up the marker. If your other foot touches down, your turn ends.
flow.kid: Toss the marker into square one. Hop on one foot through the row. Turn and hop back. Pick up the marker.

ask.q: What happens when your other foot touches the floor?
good: My turn ends.
I have broken the rule, and the next player goes.

flow.do: Tell your child that this game has many names. It is nondi or paandi in Tamil Nadu and kunte bille in Karnataka. It is tokkudu billa in Telugu and ekka dokka in Bengal. In the north it is kith-kith or stapu. Ask which name your family uses.
flow.say: This game has many names. In Tamil Nadu it is nondi or paandi. In Karnataka it is kunte bille. In Bengal it is ekka dokka. What do we call it?
flow.kid: Listen to the names of this game. Which name does your family use?

flow.do: Ask what is the same about all the names, and what is different. Ask if the rules must be exactly the same everywhere.
flow.say: The game has many names. Are the rules exactly the same in every place? Who decides?
flow.kid: Same game, many names. Are the rules the same everywhere?

ask.q: Are the rules the same in every place?
good: No, each group agrees on its own rules.
Some rules are the same, such as hopping on one foot.

activities.think: If you made one new rule for this game, what would it be, and would everyone agree?

activities.title: Keep the Balloon Up Together
activities.context: In this activity two players keep a balloon in the air together. You find out what a game feels like when you both win or both lose.

materials.item: a balloon, or a soft ball made of rolled newspaper in a sock

schedule.what: Keep the balloon up and count, then change one rule together.

activities.record: Write the highest number of taps you reached, and say how it felt to win together.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up in a living room keeping a red balloon in the air with their open hands.
setup.caption: 1. Both of you keep the balloon up.

setup.art: A tally of tap marks on a sheet of paper, with the last mark circled and two thumbs up.
setup.caption: 2. Count together. Your goal is thirty.

flow.do: Blow up the balloon and tie it yourself. Say the rule: you take turns to hit the balloon up, and you count aloud. If it touches the floor, you both lose and start again from zero. If you reach thirty, you both win.
flow.say: We are on the same side. We count each hit aloud. If the balloon touches the floor, we both start again. At thirty, we both win.
flow.kid: Hit the balloon up in turns. Count aloud. At thirty, you both win.

flow.do: Play. Start again from zero each time the balloon falls. After your first win, change one rule together. For example, hit the balloon only with an elbow. Say the new rule aloud before you start.
flow.say: Let us play. If it falls, we start again. When we reach thirty, we will change one rule.
flow.kid: Keep the balloon up. Count aloud. When you win, change one rule.
flow.parent: If the balloon pops, pick up every piece at once. Pieces of a balloon can choke a baby.

flow.do: Ask who won and who lost. Ask how this game is different from a game where one player wins.
flow.say: Who won this game? Who lost? How is it different from a race?
flow.kid: Who won? Who lost? How is this different from a race?

ask.q: How is this game different from a race?
good: We were on the same side.
We won together or lost together.

activities.think: Can a game where everybody wins still be a game? What makes it one?
activities.safety: A burst balloon can choke a baby. Pick up every piece and keep balloons away from children under five.

activities.title: Luck or Skill?
activities.context: In this activity you play one game that depends on chance and one that depends on practice. You find out which one gets better when you try again.

materials.item: a dice, or six slips of paper numbered 1 to 6 in a bowl
a rolled-up sock
a bucket or a big bowl
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Roll the dice ten times, toss the sock ten times, practise, then toss ten times again.

activities.record: Write your two sock scores. Put a tick beside the game where practice helped.

setup.art: A child rolling a white dice on a mat, with a paper tally of numbers beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Roll the dice ten times and write each number.

setup.art: A child tossing a rolled sock into a bucket one big step away, with a tally of ticks on paper.
setup.caption: 2. Toss the sock ten times. Count how many go in.

flow.do: Roll the dice ten times, or draw a slip and put it back each time. Write each number. Then try hard to make a six come up, and see what happens.
flow.say: Roll the dice ten times. Write every number. Now try as hard as you can to roll a six.
flow.kid: Roll ten times. Write each number. Try to roll a six on purpose.

ask.q: Can you make the dice show a six by trying hard?
good: No, the dice decides.
Sometimes it comes, but not because I tried.

flow.do: Put the bucket one big step away. Toss the sock ten times and count the tosses that land inside. Then practise for one minute. Then toss ten more times and count again.
flow.say: Toss the sock into the bucket ten times. Count the ones that go in. Practise for one minute. Then do ten tosses again.
flow.kid: Toss the sock ten times. Count. Practise. Toss ten more times. Count again.
flow.parent: Most children score a little higher the second time. If your child does not, that is a real result. Ask what they could change, such as how hard they throw.

flow.do: Compare the two games. Ask which one practice changed, and which one practice could not change.
flow.say: Which game did practice help? Which game did practice not help?
flow.kid: Which game got better with practice? Which game did not?

ask.q: Which game was luck, and which was skill?
good: The dice was luck.
The sock toss was skill, because practice helped.

activities.think: Is there a game you know that needs both luck and skill? What is the luck and what is the skill?

activities.title: The Safe Place Walk
activities.context: In this activity you walk through your home and find which places are safe for running games and which are not.

materials.item: a pencil
2 sheets of paper

schedule.what: Walk round, find safe and unsafe places, then practise the stop word.

activities.record: Draw one safe place and one unsafe place. Write the body part each rule protects.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up walking slowly through a flat, pointing at a wide clear floor.
setup.caption: 1. Walk slowly and look at every floor.

setup.art: A wet bathroom floor with a puddle and a red cross drawn beside it, and a dry hall with a green tick.
setup.caption: 2. A wet floor is not safe. A clear dry floor is.

flow.do: Walk slowly through your home with your child. Point to three places where a running game would be safe, and two where it would not. Look at the floor, the corners and the stairs.
flow.say: Let us walk through the house. Where would a running game be safe? Where would it not be safe? Look at the floor first.
flow.kid: Walk through your home. Find three safe places and two places that are not safe.

ask.q: Why is that place not safe for running?
good: The floor is wet and I could slip.
There are stairs and I could fall.
The corner sticks out and I could hit my head.

flow.parent: Likely answers are a wet bathroom floor, stairs, a balcony edge, a table corner and a rug that slides. Do not let your child go near a balcony edge or a kitchen stove.

flow.do: Agree on a stop word. Then run on the spot while you call out 'Go' and 'Stop' in any order. When you hear the stop word, everyone freezes at once.
flow.say: Let us agree on a stop word. When I say it, we freeze like statues. Ready? Run on the spot!
flow.kid: Pick a stop word. When you hear it, freeze at once.

ask.q: What does the stop word protect?
good: Anyone who is hurt or scared.
Everybody, because the game stops.

flow.do: Match each rule to the body part it protects. Looking at the floor protects knees and heads. Touching and never pushing protects backs and wrists. The stop word protects whoever is hurt or scared.
flow.say: Looking at the floor keeps our knees and heads safe. Touching and not pushing keeps our backs and wrists safe. Which rule do you want to keep most?
flow.kid: Each safety rule protects a part of the body. Tell your grown-up which one.

ask.q: Which rule protects knees and heads?
good: Look at the floor first.

activities.think: Is there a game you love that has a hazard in it that you cannot see? How would you find it?

activities.title: The Play Bow
activities.context: In this activity you act like two dogs who ask each other to play. You find out how a signal keeps a game friendly.

materials.item: a soft cushion or a mat

schedule.what: Do the play bow, play softly, and stop when someone says the stop word.

activities.record: Draw a dog doing a play bow. Write what the bow says in your own words.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child on a mat, both on their hands and knees with their bottoms in the air, facing each other.
setup.caption: 1. The play bow: front down, back end up.

setup.art: The child gently chasing the grown-up round the cushion, both laughing, with soft open hands.
setup.caption: 2. After the bow, play softly. Stop when anyone says Stop.

flow.do: Tell your child how dogs ask to play. One dog drops her front legs flat and keeps her back end in the air. This is a play bow. It tells the other dog that what comes next is play. Show the bow on your hands and knees.
flow.say: Dogs have a signal for play. She drops her front legs flat and keeps her back end up. It says, I am not going to hurt you. Let us play.
flow.kid: Get on your hands and knees. Put your front down and your back end up. That is the play bow.

flow.do: One of you does the play bow. The other bows back. Then play a slow, soft chase round the cushion for one minute. Touch gently, never push. Agree a stop word first. Swap who bows first.
flow.say: I bow first. You bow back. Then we chase round the cushion with soft hands. If either of us says the stop word, we stop. Then you bow first.
flow.kid: Bow first. Your partner bows back. Chase gently. Stop at the stop word.

ask.q: How did you know the chase was play?
good: We both bowed first.
We touched softly and stopped at the stop word.

flow.parent: Use a soft floor or a mat. Keep the chase slow, and keep it short.

flow.do: Ask why a dog needs a signal at all, and what happens if one dog bites too hard.
flow.say: Why do you think a dog bows before a game? What happens if one bites too hard?
flow.kid: Why does a dog bow before a game? What happens if a bite is too hard?

ask.q: Why do dogs bow before they play?
good: So the other dog knows it is play.
So nobody gets frightened.

activities.think: Do you ever have a signal with a friend that means 'this is play'? What is it?

activities.title: Six Laddus: What Is Fair?
activities.context: In this activity you share six pretend laddus in three different ways. Then you decide which way feels fair to you.

materials.item: 6 seeds, buttons or small paper circles for laddus
2 or 3 soft toys, or two family members

schedule.what: Share the six laddus three ways and say which way feels fair.

activities.record: Draw the way you think is fairest, with the laddus.

setup.art: Six brown paper circles on a steel plate, with two soft toys sitting in front of the plate.
setup.caption: 1. Six pretend laddus and two sharers.

setup.art: Three heaps of laddus in front of three soft toys, with one toy having a bigger heap.
setup.caption: 2. Three ways to share: the same, more for who needs, more for who did more.

flow.do: Put six pretend laddus on a plate. Two soft toys wait. Share them so each toy gets the same number. Count aloud. Then put them back on the plate.
flow.say: Six laddus and two friends. Share them so each friend gets the same. How many does each get?
flow.kid: Share six laddus between two toys. Give each toy the same number. Count.

flow.do: Now say that one toy missed lunch. Share the laddus again, so that the hungry toy gets more. Then say that one toy rolled all the laddus. Share again, so that the toy who helped gets more.
flow.say: Now one friend missed lunch. Share the laddus so she gets more. Now one friend helped to roll the laddus. Share the laddus so that friend gets more.
flow.kid: Share again. One toy missed lunch. Then share again. One toy helped to roll the laddus.

flow.do: Ask which of the three ways feels fair. Do not say which is right. Ask if the other toys might think differently.
flow.say: You shared three ways. Which way feels fair to you? Might another child think differently?
flow.kid: Which way feels fair? Might somebody else choose a different way?

ask.q: Which way of sharing feels fair to you, and why?
good: The same for everyone, because nobody is left out.
More for the hungry one, because she needs more.
More for the one who helped, because she did more.

flow.parent: All three answers are real ideas of fair, and grown-ups still disagree about them. Ask for a reason, and do not mark one right.

activities.think: Is there a time when the same for everyone does not feel fair? Tell about it.

activities.title: Well Played: the Soft-Toy Match
activities.context: In this activity two soft toys play one round of a game. You practise what to say when you win, and what to say when you lose.

materials.item: 2 soft toys
a dice, or two paper slips numbered 1 to 6

schedule.what: Play a toy match, practise kind words, and swap the toys' parts.

activities.record: Write or say the kind words you chose for the winner and for the loser.

setup.art: Two soft toys on a mat facing each other with a dice between them, one toy with its paws in the air.
setup.caption: 1. Each toy rolls the dice. The higher number wins.

setup.art: The losing toy with its head down and the winning toy patting its shoulder, with a speech bubble saying Well played.
setup.caption: 2. The winner says something kind. The loser breathes and tries again.

flow.do: Each toy rolls the dice once, and the higher number wins. Speak for the losing toy in a cross voice: 'That is not fair! I will never play again!' Then stop and look at your child.
flow.say: The toy on the left rolled a two. The toy on the right rolled a five. The first toy is cross and says she will never play again. What could the winner toy say?
flow.kid: One toy lost. She is cross. What could the winning toy say?

flow.do: Help your child choose kind words, such as 'Well played'. Say what the losing toy feels, which is a hot face and a tight chest. Tell her those feelings are real, and they pass.
flow.say: Losing can make a face hot and a chest tight. Those feelings are real, and they pass. What kind words will the winner say? What will the loser say?
flow.kid: Losing can feel hot and tight. It passes. Pick kind words for the winner and the loser.

ask.q: What could a kind winner say?
good: Well played.
Do you want to play again?

ask.q: What could a kind loser say?
good: Well played.
Can we play again?

flow.do: Swap the parts. Your child's toy loses now, and your toy says the kind words. Ask whether the winner could have played without the loser.
flow.say: Now the other toy loses. This toy says the kind words. Could the winner have played a game with nobody to lose?
flow.kid: Swap the parts. Say the kind words. Could the winner play with nobody to lose?

ask.q: Could the winner have a game with nobody to lose?
good: No, you need somebody to play against.
The loser helped make the game.

activities.think: What would you most like to hear when you lose a game?

projects.title: Our Family's Game Book
projects.context: In this project you ask a grown-up about a game they played as a child. You draw it, write its rules and play it.

materials.item: a few sheets of paper, stapled or folded into a little book
pencils or crayons
a grown-up to ask: a grandparent, an older relative, a neighbour or a friend's family, in person or by phone

schedule.what: Ask a grown-up about the game they played as a child, and write down its name and rules.
Draw the game and write its rules in your game book.
Play the game, then add one thing that surprised you.

projects.record: Your game book has one page for the game: its name, where it was played, its rules and a drawing. Add a line about what you changed or found.

setup.art: A child and an older neighbour sitting on a doorstep, the child writing on a small paper book.
setup.caption: 1. Ask about a game they played as a child.

setup.art: A page of a little book with a drawing of children in a lane and three short rules beside it.
setup.caption: 2. One page for the game: name, rules and a drawing.

flow.do: Help your child ask: 'What game did you play as a child? What was it called? What were the rules?' Write the answers. Ask if the game had other names in other places.
flow.say: We are going to ask someone about a game from their childhood. What was it called? Where did you play it? What were the rules?
flow.kid: Ask: what game did you play as a child? What was it called? What were the rules?

ask.q: What was the game called, and what was its main rule?
good: It had a name and a rule that everyone agreed on.

flow.do: Help your child draw the game and write its rules, one under each other. Ask if the rules are clear enough for a stranger to play.
flow.say: Let us put the game into your book. Draw the place and the players. Then write each rule, one at a time.
flow.kid: Draw the game in your book. Write each rule under the drawing.
flow.parent: If the rules are unclear, ask the person you asked, or check with a friend. A rule that two people understand differently is worth noticing.

flow.do: Play the game together, or with friends, on the day. After one round, ask what in the game surprised your child, and whether the rules worked.
flow.say: Now we play the game from your book. Does every rule work? What surprised you?
flow.kid: Play the game from your book. Did every rule work? What surprised you?

ask.q: Did every rule work when you played?
good: Yes.
One rule was unclear, so we agreed a new one.

projects.think: If a game has been played for a hundred years, who made its rules?

projects.title: Make Our Own Game with Three Rules
projects.context: In this project you invent a game with a goal and three rules, play it, and change one rule.

materials.item: 10 seeds or dried beans
a small bowl and a sheet of paper
a friend or a grown-up to play with

schedule.what: Invent a game with a goal and three rules, and write the rules down.
Play the game, notice a rule that is unclear, change it and play again.

projects.record: Your rule page has the game's name, its goal and its three rules. Add the rule you changed and why.

setup.art: A child at a mat with ten seeds, a bowl and a sheet of paper with the heading GOAL and three numbered lines.
setup.caption: 1. Invent a goal and three rules.

setup.art: Two children playing the game on the mat, one pointing at a rule written on the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Play it. Change one rule if it is unclear.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose a goal, such as 'get all the seeds into the bowl first'. Then ask for three rules. Write them. Ask if a stranger could play from the rules alone.
flow.say: Let us invent a game. First pick a goal. Then make three rules. Then I will write them down.
flow.kid: Pick a goal. Make three rules. Your grown-up writes them.

ask.q: What is the goal of your game?
good: A clear sentence, such as 'get seven seeds in the bowl first'.

flow.do: Play the game with a friend or with you. If a rule is unclear or unfair, stop and change it. Say the new rule aloud, make sure that everyone agrees, and play again.
flow.say: Let us play your game. If something is not clear, we stop and fix the rule. Everyone must agree to the new rule.
flow.kid: Play your game. If a rule is unclear, change it. Everyone must agree.

ask.q: Which rule did you change, and why?
good: One that was unclear.
One that was unfair to one player.

flow.parent: A game whose first version has a flaw is normal. Fixing the flaw with everybody agreeing is the lesson.

projects.think: Which rule of your game would be hardest to keep when you are losing?

challenges.title: A Fair Start for a Big Child and a Small Child
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a rule for a race so that a child of ten and a child of six both have a real chance to win.
challenges.problem: A girl of ten and a boy of six want to race across a room. If they start at the same line, she wins every time. Make a rule so that each of them has a real chance to win.
constraints: Both children must agree to the rule before the race.
The rule must fit in one or two sentences, said aloud.
Race on a dry floor with a clear path, or outside.
There is more than one good rule. Try at least two.
materials: a strip of tape or a chalk line
a shoe or a toy as a finishing mark
a dupatta or cloth for a second line
a timer or a clock with a seconds hand
general: Give the younger child a head start of a few steps.
Let the older child hop on one foot while the younger child runs.
Make the older child run further, to a mark that is more steps away.
creative: Both children race a clock instead of each other, and then they compare times.
The older child must carry a pillow, and the younger child must not.
After one race, the winner gives the other child a bigger head start, so each race is closer than the last.
challenges.your_turn: Try two different rules. Race three times with each. Which rule made both of you want to race again? Say why.
challenges.safety: Race on a dry floor with the path clear of furniture, or outdoors. Agree a stop word first.

setup.art: Two lines of tape on a floor with a gate-like toy at the far end, a tall girl at one line and a small boy a few steps ahead of her.
setup.caption: 1. A race from two different lines.

setup.art: A child writing a rule on a sheet of paper with a drawing of two runners and a number of steps.
setup.caption: 2. Write your rule in one or two sentences.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Show the finishing mark and the two lines. Ask what rule might help a six-year-old and a ten-year-old both have a chance.
flow.say: A big child and a small child want to race. If they start together, the big child always wins. What rule could make it a real race?
flow.kid: A big child and a small child will race. Think of a rule that gives both a chance.

ask.q: What rule could make the race fair for both?
good: A head start for the small child.
The big child hops.
The big child runs further.

flow.do: Try your child's first rule. Race three times and count who wins each time. Say the rule aloud before you start. Both players must agree.
flow.say: Let us try your rule. Say it aloud. Do we both agree? Now race three times.
flow.kid: Say your rule aloud. Both players agree. Race three times. Count who wins.
flow.parent: Count the wins as 'big child' and 'small child'. If one always wins, the rule needs a change.

flow.do: Change the rule once, using one of the ideas above or your own. Race three more times. Ask which rule was closer, and which made them both want to race again.
flow.say: Now change one thing in the rule. Race three times more. Which rule made a closer race?
flow.kid: Change one thing in your rule. Race three more times. Which race was closer?

ask.q: Which rule made a closer race?
good: The one with a head start.
A rule that both players picked together.

challenges.title: Build a Safe Place for a Rolling Game
challenges.context: This is a building challenge. A ball keeps rolling under the sofa, so you build a small play place on the floor that keeps the ball in and the players safe.
challenges.problem: You want to play a rolling game on the floor with a small ball, but the ball keeps rolling away under furniture. Build a play place so that the ball stays inside and nobody can slip or trip.
constraints: Use only things you already have at home.
The walls must be low enough for hands to reach in.
The ball must stay inside at least eight times out of ten rolls.
Nothing may hang over the edge where feet could trip on it.
materials: a small soft ball or a ball of scrunched paper
general: Make a square wall of books on a rug.
Put cushions in a ring so the ball bounces back.
Use a big cardboard box laid on its side as a pitch.
creative: Slope one side of the pitch a little, so the ball rolls back to the players by itself.
Make a gap in one wall as a goal, and a roll through it earns a point.
Fold a blanket into a long tunnel for the ball to roll through.
challenges.your_turn: Test your play place with ten rolls. Count how many stay inside. Change one thing and test again. What changed the count?

setup.art: A square of books and cushions on a rug in a flat, with a small ball inside and a sofa behind it.
setup.caption: 1. Build the walls round the play place.

setup.art: A child rolling a small ball across the square while a grown-up counts on fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Roll ten times. Count the rolls that stay inside.

flow.do: Read the problem. Show the floor space and the things to use. Ask where the ball escapes in a game like this one.
flow.say: The ball keeps rolling under the sofa. We want a place where the ball stays in and nobody trips. What could make a wall?
flow.kid: The ball keeps rolling away. What could you use to make a wall?

ask.q: What could stop a ball from rolling away?
good: A wall of books.
Cushions.
A box.

flow.do: Build the first play place. Roll the ball ten times from one end. Count the rolls that stay inside. Write the number.
flow.say: Build your walls. Then roll the ball ten times. Count how many stay inside.
flow.kid: Build walls. Roll ten times. Count how many stay in.
flow.parent: Check that no wall or blanket sticks out where feet might trip. Keep the walls low.

flow.do: Change one thing, using one of the ideas above or your own. Roll ten more times and count again. Ask what changed the count.
flow.say: Change one thing about the walls. Roll again ten times. Did the count change?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Roll ten more times. Count again.

ask.q: What did you change, and did the count change?
good: I made the walls higher, so extra rolls stayed in.
I added a cushion, and the ball bounced back.

items.p: Which of these is a rule?
items.why: A rule says what players may do or must do. The colour of the floor or the seeds is not a rule.

items.p: Ten seeds on the floor are already a game.
items.why: False. The seeds become a game only when the players agree on a rule and keep it.

items.p: A grown-up reads each game. Is it an indoor game or an outdoor game?
items.why: Indoor games fit in a room, and outdoor games need open space for running.

items.p: Draw a line from each rule to what it does.
items.why: Each rule has a job. A strong answer can say what would go wrong without the rule.

items.p: In a game, all the players agree to keep the ____.
items.why: A game is play with rules that all the players agree to keep.

items.p: Name a game you like. Say one rule of it. Say your answer aloud, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: A real game and one real rule of it, such as 'In hide and seek, the seeker counts to twenty.'
items.why: A strong answer names a real game and gives one rule that every player keeps.

items.p: Put these in order for a game. A grown-up reads them.
items.why: The players agree on the rules first. They play next. They say kind words when it ends.

items.p: Draw two children taking turns. Show whose go it is now.
items.a: Two children, one acting and one waiting, with a sign or a pointing finger to show whose turn it is.
items.why: A strong drawing shows one player acting and the other waiting, which is what a turn is.

items.p: A player who loses is a bad player.
items.why: False. The player who loses has helped to make the game. Without a second player, nobody could win.

items.p: Meera, aged six, and her cousin Arun, aged ten, choose how to play ludo. A grown-up reads what each says.

views.says: Turns should go round the table, so that everyone gets a go.
The oldest should go first, because the oldest knows the rules best.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Say one good thing about the other idea.
items.a: A good answer picks a side with a reason, and names one good thing about the other idea, such as that Arun's idea gives a clear start.
items.why: Each idea can be defended. Going round the table shares the turns. An oldest-first rule gives an easy start, but it may leave the younger child waiting.

items.p: Three of these keep players safe. Which one does not?
items.why: Stairs are not safe for a running game. The other three are safety rules.

items.p: Ten seeds are in a heap. A player takes 2. How many seeds are left?
items.why: 10 take away 2 is 8.

items.p: In snakes and ladders the dice decides every move. Who has the best chance of winning?
opts: Every player has the same chance
items.why: The dice does not know who is old or fast. Each player has the same chance on each roll.

items.p: Chess has no dice. What mostly decides who wins?
items.why: Every move in chess is a choice. The player who plans better usually wins, so chess is mostly a game of skill.

items.p: Is each game mostly luck, mostly skill, or both?
items.why: Dice-only games depend on luck. Games of choices and practice depend on skill. Many games have some of each.

items.p: A child cheats at ludo. What does the cheat need the other players to do?
items.why: A cheat gains only if the others keep the rule. If everyone cheated, nobody would get ahead.

items.p: Everybody agrees on one meaning of 'fair'.
items.why: False. Some people say fair means the same for everyone. Others say it means more for who needs more, or more for who did more.

items.p: Two children share six laddus. Say one way that could be fair, and why. A grown-up writes your answer.
items.a: Any way with a reason, such as 'Three each, so that nobody has more' or 'The hungry child gets one more, because she needs more'.
items.why: A strong answer gives a way to share and a reason for it. More than one answer can be fair.

items.p: Six laddus. One child missed lunch. A grown-up reads what each friend says.

views.says: Everyone gets the same, so nobody is left out.
The child who missed lunch gets one more, because she needs it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why?
items.a: Either side with a reason. A strong answer also says what is good in the other idea.
items.why: Anita's idea treats everyone the same. Karim's idea looks at what each child needs. Grown-ups and scientists still disagree about which kind of fair is better.

items.p: Draw a game where everyone wins together. Show what the players do.
items.a: Players on one side working at one goal, such as keeping a balloon up.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the players on the same side, with one goal that all of them reach or miss together.

items.p: Draw a line from each game to its kind.
pairs: Keeping a balloon up together, and both lose if it falls
Each side flicks carrom coins to pocket them
items.why: In a cooperative game the players are on one side. In a competitive game each player or team tries to beat the others.

items.p: A big dog rolls onto her back so a puppy can be on top. What is she doing?
opts: Keeping the play fair for the small one
items.why: Big dogs hold back their strength so that small dogs can join the play. Then they swap, which is turn-taking.

items.p: A ____ rule is a rule that keeps players from getting hurt.
items.why: A safety rule protects bodies, for example looking at the floor first or agreeing a stop word.

items.p: A dog is doing a play bow. A grown-up points to each part. What does the dog do with each part?
items.why: In a play bow the front legs go flat and the back end goes up. It is a signal that means 'This is play.'
items.art: A street dog in a play bow, front legs flat on the ground, back end in the air and tail up, with an empty label beside each part.

items.p: Before a game starts, all the players agree to change a rule. Is that cheating?
items.why: Rules are made by players, so players can change them. Cheating is breaking a rule in secret.

items.p: Ten seeds. Take one or two a turn. The last seed wins. You go first. How many do you take?
items.why: Take 1 and leave 9. Then each time your friend takes 1, you take 2. Each time your friend takes 2, you take 1. The seeds go 9, 6, 3, 0, and you take the last.

items.p: A game can still be a game if only one player keeps the rule.
items.why: False. The other player is then playing something else, so the two players no longer share one game.

items.p: A big sister lets her small brother win at ludo without telling him. Is that kind? Give one reason.
items.a: Either answer with a reason, such as 'Kind, because he enjoys it' or 'Not honest, because he does not know the truth'.
items.why: Both sides have a real point. A good answer also thinks about how the small brother would feel when he finds out.

items.p: Is a little risk in play good for children? A grown-up reads what each person says.

views.says: A child who climbs a little too high and wobbles learns how high is too high.

views.who: A doctor who treats broken arms
views.says: Falls hurt many children, so we should lower the frames and put down soft ground.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What would you ask the other side?
items.a: Either side with a reason, or a middle path. A strong answer says what would be lost on the other side.
items.why: Scientists still disagree about this. Both sides want children to be well. They disagree about where the line is.

items.p: Three are hazards a child cannot see. Which one is a risk a child can see?
opts: A wet patch under a rug
A loose slab on a wall
The height of a low branch
A crack in a plastic chair
items.why: A hazard is a danger the child cannot see. A branch's height is something the child can see and judge.

items.p: Draw two ways to start a race so that a child of six and a child of ten both have a chance.
items.a: One drawing with a head start for the younger child, and one with another way, such as the older child going further.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two different starts, and the starts are not the same line for both children.

items.p: Scientists found that rats learned hide and seek when the only reward was being tickled. What does this suggest?
opts: Play can be its own reward
Play always needs a food prize
items.why: The rats had no food prize and still learned the game. So play seems to reward itself.

items.p: Scientists have agreed on exactly what play is.
items.why: False. Scientists use working tests such as five signs, but they have no final agreed meaning of play.

items.p: Is each one a game rule, a safety rule or cheating?
items: Say the stop word to freeze the game
Peek during the counting in hide and seek
Take one seed or two seeds on your turn
Run only on a dry floor
Move four squares when the dice shows three
items.why: A game rule says how to play. A safety rule keeps bodies safe. Cheating breaks a rule in secret.

items.p: Why does a winner need the player who lost? Say it in your own words.
items.a: A good answer says that winning needs somebody who played against you, so the loser helps to make the game.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the other player is half of the game. Without a second player, there is nobody to beat.

items.p: Which is a hazard rather than a risk?
opts: A child jumps from the second step
A rug hides a wet floor
A child climbs onto a low wall
items.why: A hazard is a danger the child cannot see. The child jumping or climbing can see and judge, which makes those risks.

quiz.p: Ten seeds lie on the floor. What turns them into a game?
opts: The players agree on a rule and keep it
quiz.why: A game exists only when the players agree to keep a rule. The seeds alone are just seeds.

quiz.p: One player changes a rule in secret halfway through. What has she done?
opts: Cheated, because the others keep the old rule
Started a new game for everyone
quiz.why: A rule can change only when all the players agree. A secret change is cheating.

quiz.p: Which game needs open space more than a small table?
quiz.why: Kho-kho means running, so it needs open space. Carrom and chess fit on a board.

quiz.p: Nondi, kunte bille and ekka dokka are names for what?
opts: One hopping game with many names
quiz.why: The same hopping game has different names in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Bengal.

quiz.p: In snakes and ladders the dice decides every move. What kind of game is this?
quiz.why: No move is a choice, so the result depends on chance.

quiz.p: Two children want the same swing. Which rule gives both a go?
opts: Take turns, with the turns counted
quiz.why: A turn rule shares the playing time. Without one, the fastest or strongest child takes every go.

quiz.p: Why is waiting for a turn easier when people keep their promises?
opts: You trust that your turn will come
quiz.why: In one study, children who had met a promise-keeper waited about four times as long as children who had met a promise-breaker.

quiz.p: A child who missed lunch gets an extra laddu. Which idea of fair is this?
opts: More for the one who needs more
More for the one who did more
quiz.why: Fair has more than one meaning. This one gives more to the child who needs more.

quiz.p: A race has a child of six and a child of ten. Which start is fair?
opts: It depends on what the race is for
quiz.why: The same line is the same for both, and a head start gives the younger child more of a chance. People still disagree.

quiz.p: Why do we look at the floor before a running game?
opts: A wet floor can hurt knees and heads
The floor must be clean for the seeds
We want to find our chappals
quiz.why: Looking at the place protects heads and knees from slips and falls.

quiz.p: A friend calls the stop word. What does everyone do?
quiz.why: The stop word protects whoever is hurt or scared, so everybody stops at once.

quiz.p: You win. Why do you need the player who lost?
opts: Winning needs someone who played against you
quiz.why: A win needs another player who tried. The player who lost helped to make the game.

quiz.p: You lose and your face feels hot and angry. What is true?
opts: The feeling is real and it passes
A good player never feels it
quiz.why: Feelings after a loss are real, and they pass. Saying 'Well played' helps both players want to play again.

quiz.p: A dog drops her front legs flat and lifts her back end. What does it mean?
opts: This is play, I am not attacking
quiz.why: It is a play bow, a signal that tells another dog that what comes next is play.

quiz.p: Which question about play has no answer yet?
opts: Why do animals play at all
How many faces a dice has
How many players are in a kabaddi team
quiz.why: Scientists have several ideas about why animals play, and none is settled.

quiz.p: Two friends keep a balloon up, and both lose if it falls. What kind of game is it?
quiz.why: Both players are on one side. They win together or lose together.

maths.problem: Ten seeds are in a heap. You take 1, and your friend takes 2. How many seeds are left?
maths.explain: 10 take away 1 is 9. Then 9 take away 2 is 7.
maths.context: This is about the ten-seed game from the Two Ways Test.
maths.why_maths: Taking away from ten shows how a turn rule brings the game closer to its end.

maths.problem: In the ten-seed game, you take 1 and leave 9. After that, each time your friend takes some seeds, you take enough to make 3 seeds in that pair of turns. How many pairs of turns until the seeds are gone?
maths.explain: Each pair of turns takes away 3 seeds. 9 seeds go 6, then 3, then 0. That is 3 pairs.
maths.context: This is about a pattern in the ten-seed game.
maths.why_maths: Counting in threes shows how a pattern can help a player to win, and it is the maths hidden in the game.

maths.problem: Six laddus are shared so that everyone gets the same. How many does each child get with 2 children? With 3 children?
maths.answer: 3 each with 2 children. 2 each with 3 children.
maths.explain: 6 shared between 2 is 3 and 3. 6 shared between 3 is 2, 2 and 2.
maths.context: This is about the six laddus.
maths.why_maths: Sharing into equal groups is the maths of 'the same for everyone', the first idea of fair.

maths.problem: A dice has the numbers 1 to 6. You need a six to win. Is a six more likely, less likely or the same as a three?
maths.explain: Each face is one of six faces and the dice has no favourite, so every number has the same chance.
maths.context: This is about the dice in the snakes and ladders game.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the chances of faces shows why a dice game is a game of luck and not of skill.

applications: In a school queue at the water tap, children take turns. The turn rule lets every child drink, not only the quickest ones.
A cricket umpire in a school or lane game keeps the rules the players agreed. Watch what the team does when there is no umpire.
Traffic lights are rules that all road users agree to keep. One driver going through on red puts the others at risk, just as in a game.
A clinic waiting room gives out number tokens so that each patient is seen in turn. Look for the token machine or the numbered slips.
On a school sports day, the rules of each race are read out first, so every runner knows them before the whistle.

jokes.j: Why is a snake so good at snakes and ladders?

jokes.j: Why was the ludo token still at home?

buy.item: Tamarind seeds, dried beans or buttons (a small packet)
buy.why: Ten of them are needed for the Two Ways Test and for the seed games. About ₹20 to ₹40. Any dried beans, rajma or chana, or ten buttons of one kind, work as well.
buy.plan: Get them before the Two Ways Test.

buy.item: Paper masking tape, or a box of chalk
buy.why: Used to mark the hopscotch squares and the race lines. About ₹30 to ₹60 a roll. A box of chalk costs about ₹10 to ₹20 for outside play, and a strip of cloth can mark a line inside.
buy.plan: Get it before Hopscotch Has Many Names.

buy.why: One is used for Keep the Balloon Up Together. About ₹20 to ₹50. A soft ball of rolled newspaper in a sock works as well.
buy.plan: Get them before Keep the Balloon Up Together.

buy.item: A dice, or a ludo set
buy.why: Used in Luck or Skill, the soft-toy match and the snakes and ladders game. About ₹10 for a dice and about ₹100 to ₹250 for a ludo set. Six paper slips numbered 1 to 6 in a bowl work as well.
buy.plan: Get one before Luck or Skill.

buy.item: Printing for the games and the worksheets
buy.why: The two games need about 3 pages, and the three worksheets about 3 pages. About ₹2 to ₹5 a page at a print shop. You may also draw the game pieces by hand.

buy.item: Free picture books about games and play (StoryWeaver)
buy.why: Free picture books in many Indian languages to read aloud. Search for games, play and friends. Costs nothing.
buy.plan: Look before the Game Book project.

quiz: A game needs rules that the players agree to keep.
A game is play with rules that all the players agree to keep.
Seeds on the floor are always a game.
The seeds become a game only when the players agree on a rule.
Kho-kho is an indoor game.
Kho-kho needs open space, so it is an outdoor game.
Taking turns gives every player a go.
A turn rule shares the playing time.
In snakes and ladders the dice decides every move.
No move is a choice, so it is a game of luck.
A cheat breaks a rule in secret.
A cheat needs the others to keep the rule.
A stop word means keep going.
A stop word means stop now, and everyone stops.
Practice can make you better at a skill.
Skill grows with practice, but luck does not.
The player who loses has no part in the game.
The player who loses helps to make the game.
Dogs have a signal to say 'let us play'.
The play bow tells another dog that what comes next is play.
odd: Carrom, chess and ludo are indoor games. Kho-kho needs open space.
Rule, turn and goal are parts of a game. A mango is a fruit.
Stairs are not safe for a running game. The others are safety rules.
Nondi, kunte bille and ekka dokka are names for hopscotch. Pallanguzhi is a game with seeds and pits.
Dice, luck and chance go together. Skill grows with practice.
